flop_classes.name: Cerebras WSE-3: what does NOT work well — capacity, flexibility, and ecosystem
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Cerebras WSE-3 limitations: (1) capacity — 44 GB SRAM per wafer is small vs GPU HBM (80-192 GB), so models >44 GB require multi-wafer pipelining; (2) no dynamic batching — the wafer-scale architecture is optimized for single-stream low-latency decode, not high-throughput batched inference; (3) limited software ecosystem — no vLLM, no PyTorch native support; uses Cerebras SDK only; (4) no fine-tuning on CS-3/CS-4 (training is separate); (5) high cost per system; (6) limited to Cerebras Cloud or on-prem deployment.
scales_with: model_size (44 GB limit per wafer)
batch_size (optimized for single-stream, not high-throughput batching)
software_ecosystem (limited vs GPU)
deployment_flexibility (Cerebras Cloud or on-prem only)

flop_classes.name: Cerebras WSE-3: wafer-scale SRAM bandwidth advantage for inference
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The WSE-3 packs 44 GB of on-chip SRAM at 21 PB/s bandwidth (CS-3) or 43.2 PB/s (CS-4 Turbo). This is ~1000x the bandwidth of GPU HBM. Weights stay on-chip — there is no weight streaming from HBM. Tokens flow uninterrupted through model layers pipelined across wafers. The bandwidth advantage is most pronounced for decode, where GPU inference is bottlenecked by memory bandwidth. Cerebras claims up to 30x faster inference than GPUs for frontier models.
scales_with: model_size (must fit in 44 GB SRAM per wafer, or be pipelined across wafers)
sram_bandwidth (21-43.2 PB/s, ~1000x GPU HBM)
num_wafers (CS-4 has 3 wafers for larger models)
token_generation_rate (up to 750 tok/s for GPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast)

flop_classes.name: Groq LPU: compiler and kernel constraints from static scheduling
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The Groq compiler is model-independent — it does not require model-specific kernel coding (unlike GPUs). It accepts workloads from multiple frameworks and maps/schedules them across one or more LPUs. The compiler outputs a program encompassing all data movement information. Constraints: (1) all shapes must be static — no dynamic shapes, (2) the entire data flow graph must be known at compile time, (3) no data-dependent control flow, (4) memory allocation is static. This means no dynamic batching, no variable-length sequences without padding, no runtime reconfiguration.
scales_with: model_complexity (more complex models = longer compilation)
num_chips (more chips = more scheduling)
sequence_length (must be static or bucketed)
batch_size (must be static)

flop_classes.name: Groq LPU: deterministic single-core-per-token architecture and SRAM-to-DRAM ratio
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The Groq LPU uses a deterministic assembly-line architecture where each token is processed by a single core (SIMD function unit) with no dynamic scheduling, no cache misses, and no variance. All data movement is statically scheduled at compile time. The SRAM-to-DRAM ratio is effectively infinite — there is no DRAM tier. 230 MB of on-chip SRAM at 80 TB/s bandwidth vs GPU HBM at ~8 TB/s. This means the memory hierarchy assumptions are completely inverted: there is no weight streaming from HBM, no cache hierarchy, no prefetching. The compiler must fit the entire model (or a tile of it) in SRAM at compile time.
scales_with: model_size (must fit in 230 MB SRAM per chip, or be tiled across chips)
sram_bandwidth (80 TB/s — 10x GPU HBM)
num_chips (larger models need more chips for capacity)
compile_time (static scheduling means longer compilation for complex models)

flop_classes.name: AWS Neuron: dtype and configuration tradeoffs for inference
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Inferentia2 supports FP32, TF32, BF16, FP16, UINT8, and cFP8 (configurable FP8). Trainium2 adds FP8 at 1300 TFLOPS per chip. The auto-cast path takes FP32/FP16 models and casts down to BF16/FP8/cFP8 at compile time. Stochastic rounding is available to protect accuracy. The dtype choice directly affects throughput: FP8 is 2x FP16 on paper, but real speedup depends on the model and whether the compiler can effectively use the lower precision.
scales_with: precision (FP32 -> BF16 -> FP8, each step changes throughput)
model_architecture (some models tolerate lower precision better)
stochastic_rounding (accuracy protection at slight performance cost)
auto_cast_vs_manual (auto-cast is easier but may not be optimal)

flop_classes.name: AWS Neuron: neuroncc compilation, NEFF format, and auto-casting
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The Neuron Graph Compiler (neuronx-cc) transforms ML models from TensorFlow/MXNet/PyTorch/XLA HLO into NEFF (Neuron Executable File Format). It auto-casts FP32 operations to BF16 by default for optimal performance. Supports optimization levels 1-3 (compilation time vs runtime performance). Model-specific optimizations for Transformer and U-Net architectures. Logical NeuronCore sharding for distributed inference. The compiler is invoked transparently through framework plugins.
scales_with: model_size (larger models = longer compilation)
optimization_level (1-3, higher = better runtime but longer compile)
precision (FP32->BF16 auto-cast, or FP8 for higher throughput)
num_neuron_cores (sharding degree affects compilation)

flop_classes.name: AWS Neuron: NRT memory model, collectives, and multi-chip inference
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The NeuronX Runtime (NRT) loads NEFF files and executes them on NeuronCores. It handles device allocation, memory management, and collective communications. For multi-chip inference, NeuronLink provides chip-to-chip bandwidth (192 GB/s for Inf2, 1024 GB/s for Trn2). The runtime supports explicit async APIs (nrta_*) for fine-grained scheduling. Collectives (AllGather, ReduceScatter, AllReduce, AlltoAll, Permute) are used for distributed inference. Intra-node collectives use NeuronLink; inter-node use EFA.
scales_with: num_chips (more chips = more communication)
neuronlink_bandwidth (192 GB/s Inf2, 1024 GB/s Trn2)
efa_bandwidth (inter-node, 3.2 Tbps for Trn2)
collective_type (AllReduce vs AllGather vs AlltoAll)

flop_classes.name: Rebellions Rebel100: 4-chiplet UCIe mesh and predictive DMA for inference
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Rebel100 uses 4 chiplets connected via UCIe-Advanced mesh at 1 TB/s per bidirectional channel at 11 ns latency. The four chiplets present as one virtual die with no software-visible boundary. 144 GB HBM3E at 4.8 TB/s. The predictive DMA engine enables 2.7 TB/s effective bandwidth for KV data prefetch on long-context decode. The inter-chiplet link, not the memory, is the architectural story — 11 ns is roughly a register-to-register hop.
scales_with: hbm3e_bandwidth (4.8 TB/s, 144 GB capacity)
ucie_mesh_bandwidth (1 TB/s per channel, 11 ns latency)
predictive_dma (2.7 TB/s effective for KV prefetch)
num_chiplets (4, presenting as one virtual die)

flop_classes.name: Tenstorrent Tensix: small-SRAM, modest-bandwidth, open-source architecture
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Tenstorrent Wormhole (n150) has 108 MB SRAM, 12 GB GDDR6 at 288 GB/s, 74 TFLOPS FP16. Blackhole (p150) has 180 MB SRAM, 32 GB GDDR6 at 512 GB/s, 664 TFLOPS BLOCKFP8. The architecture uses Tensix cores with dedicated RISC-V control cores and a network-on-chip. SRAM acts as a L2-like feed tier. The design bets on very low power (160-300 W) and open-source software rather than winning the bandwidth race. For inference, it is decisively bandwidth-bound at batch 1.
scales_with: sram_capacity (108-180 MB, acts as L2)
gddr6_bandwidth (288-512 GB/s, the wall for batch-1 decode)
num_tensix_cores (72-120 per ASIC)
power_consumption (160-300 W, very low)

flop_classes.name: TPU bucketing and padding: batch size rules for MXU efficiency
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The TPU runtime splits a batch across all 8 cores of a TPU device. For v5e/v5p/v6e, each core uses 8x128 vector registers. Batch size should be evenly divisible by 8 or 128. The XLA compiler rounds up tensor sizes in HBM for efficiency. Two rules: (1) batch multiple of 64 with feature dims multiple of 128, OR (2) batch multiple of 1024 with feature dims multiple of 8. Batch 1024 with feature dims multiple of 128 gives best efficiency.
scales_with: batch_size (the primary knob — must align to 64 or 1024)
feature_dimensions (must align to 128 or 8)
num_tpu_cores (8 per host, batch splits across cores)
mxu_tile_size (128x128 for pre-v6e, 256x256 for v6e+)

flop_classes.name: TPU MFU: performance guide rules for achieving good model flops utilization
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) on TPU is governed by: (1) input-bound models — ensure steady data stream with parallel reads, (2) small batch from sharding — use largest batch that fits, (3) memory management — TPU_PREMAPPED_BUFFER_SIZE tuning, pinned_host vs unpinned_host, (4) network — MTU 8896, multi-NIC for multislice, (5) XLA optimizations — padding, tensor dimensions > MXU size, batch size rules, fusion, broadcasting. For TPU7x: FP8 gives 1.3x over BF16, rematerialization costs 25-30% FLOPs, SparseCore collective offloading overlaps communication.
scales_with: batch_size (larger batch = better MXU utilization)
data_pipeline (input-bound if data cannot be loaded fast enough)
precision (FP8 doubles peak FLOPs vs BF16 on TPU7x)
rematerialization_policy (25-30% FLOPs overhead for memory savings)
communication_overhead (FSDP all-gather, EP all-to-all)

flop_classes.name: TPU SPMD partitioning: how layout constrains model architecture
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: TPUs use SPMD (Single Program, Multiple Data) where the same program runs on all cores. The XLA compiler automatically partitions tensors across cores using layout constraints. This means the model architecture must be amenable to automatic sharding — manual control is limited compared to GPU tensor parallelism. The compiler inserts collectives (all-reduce, all-gather) automatically, but the sharding strategy is constrained by the SPMD model.
scales_with: num_cores (more cores = more sharding)
tensor_dimensions (must be divisible by core count for even sharding)
model_architecture (some architectures shard cleanly, others do not)
ici_bandwidth (inter-chip interconnect bandwidth bounds collective cost)

flop_classes.name: TPU XLA compilation: static shapes, padding, and fusion
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: XLA compiles the entire HLO graph to a TPU executable at compile time. All tensor shapes must be known statically — there is no dynamic shape support. The compiler pads tensors to 128x8 chunks (the MXU tile size); padding wastes compute and memory. Batch size must be a multiple of 64 (8 per core) with feature dims multiple of 128, OR batch multiple of 1024 with feature dims multiple of 8. Fusion eliminates intermediate HBM round-trips. Broadcasting can force materialization and prevent fusion.
scales_with: batch_size (must be multiple of 64 or 1024 for efficiency)
feature_dimensions (must be multiple of 128 or 8)
tensor_shapes (must be static — no dynamic shapes)
fusion_opportunities (more fusion = less HBM traffic)

flop_classes.name: FlashAttention-3 vs FA-4: register pressure vs shared-memory bandwidth bottleneck distinction
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: FA-3 and FA-4 attack different bottlenecks. FA-3 (Hopper): the bottleneck is SFU/matmul overlap. On H100 SXM5, tensor cores do 989 TFLOPS FP16 but only 3.9 TFLOPS of special functions (16 ops/SM/clock * 132 SM * 1.83 GHz). At head_dim 128, there are ~512x more matmul than exponential FLOPs, so without overlap, exp can take 50% of the time of the matmuls. In FP8 it gets worse because matmul doubles while exp does not. FA-3 reduces register pressure to address this: warp specialization (producer warps issue TMA, consumer warps issue WGMMA), ping-pong two warpgroups with bar.sync, 2-stage pipelining. FA-3 achieves 740 TFLOPs/s FP16 (75% of peak), 1.2 PFLOPs/s FP8. FA-4 (Blackwell): the bottleneck moves to shared-memory bandwidth in the backward pass. Per B200 SM at M=N=D=128: tensor cores 8192 ops/cycle, exponential unit 16 ops/cycle, shared memory 128 bytes/cycle. Forward per tile: 1024 tensor-core cycles vs 1024 exp cycles vs 768 SMEM cycles - forward is bound by compute AND exponential simultaneously. Backward (5 chained MMAs): 2560 tensor-core, 1024 exp, 3328 SMEM - backward is bound by SHARED-MEMORY BANDWIDTH, not FLOPs. FA-4 addresses this with: tcgen05 UMMA with TMEM accumulators (removes register pressure), 2-CTA MMA (halves operand-B SMEM traffic), emulated exp (Cody-Waite + Horner polynomial on FMA units), conditional online-softmax rescaling. FA-4 achieves 1605 TFLOPs/s BF16 on B200 (71% of 2250 TFLOPS peak).
scales_with: head_dim (exp cost per matmul flop scales inversely with head_dim)
precision (fp8 doubles tensor-core flops but leaves SFU exp unchanged)
seqlen
batch_size

flop_classes.name: FlashAttention 1-4 generation comparison: what each changed mechanically and measured performance
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Each FA generation attacks a different bottleneck. FA-1 (2022): IO-aware tiling eliminates S x S HBM round trip, 2-4x wallclock vs PyTorch. FA-2 (2023): work partitioning fix, ~2x vs FA-1, 50-73% of peak FLOPs/s on A100 (FA-1 was 25-40%). FA-3 (2024): Hopper warp specialization + TMA + FP8, 1.5-2.0x vs FA-2, 740 TFLOPs/s FP16 (75% of 989 TFLOPS peak), ~1.2 PFLOPs/s FP8 on H100. FA-4 (2025): Blackwell tcgen05 UMMA + TMEM + 2-CTA MMA + emulated exp, up to 1605 TFLOPs/s BF16 on B200 (71% of 2250 TFLOPS peak). The progression: FA-1 fixes bytes, FA-2 fixes scheduling, FA-3 fixes SFU/matmul overlap, FA-4 fixes shared-memory bandwidth in backward. Each generation is arch-specific: FA-1 works on Ampere+, FA-2 adds better Ampere/Ada, FA-3 requires Hopper (wgmma + TMA), FA-4 requires Blackwell (tcgen05 + TMEM).
scales_with: context_length (tiling efficiency scales with L)
head_dim (FA-3/4 warp specialization tuned for 128/256)
precision (FA-3 FP8 doubles tensor-core flops but SFU exp unchanged)
num_SMs (FA-2 partitioning, FA-4 2-CTA MMA needs CTA pairs)

flop_classes.name: Low-rank key projection and KV compression: research-only vs deployed
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Low-rank key projection and KV compression aim to reduce the KV cache by projecting to a lower-dimensional space. MLA (Multi-head Latent Attention) is the deployed extreme of this: it compresses K and V JOINTLY through one shared down-projection W_DKV, so every head's K and V live in the same d_c-dimensional subspace. MLA is deployed in DeepSeek-V2/V3/V4. GQA/MQA reduce cache by reducing KV head count - GQA is universally deployed, MQA is widely used. Low-rank key projection (separate from MLA) is research-only: no production engine ships a general low-rank KV projection. KV quantization (fp8/int8/int4) is deployed: FlashMLA supports fp8/fp4 KV cache on Blackwell. KV compression via token merging (e.g., PyramidKV, SnapKV, H2O) is research-only: they reduce the number of cached tokens but require a selection pass and are not in production engines.
scales_with: context_length (KV cache bytes scale linearly)
num_kv_heads (GQA/MQA reduce head count)
kv_lora_rank d_c (MLA cache elements per token)
kv_cache_dtype (fp8/fp4/int8 quantization)

flop_classes.name: MLA kernel support matrix: which architectures and engines support Multi-head Latent Attention
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: MLA kernel support is arch-specific and engine-specific. FlashMLA (DeepSeek's kernel library) requires NVIDIA SM100/SM103 (Blackwell) with CUDA >= 13.1. The 2026.09.30 release REMOVED Hopper support and earlier models (V3/V3.2/V4.0). Decode supports only FP8 and FP4 KV cache - bf16 KV is explicitly NOT supported. On Hopper, an older FlashMLA checkout is required. vLLM integrates FlashMLA for DeepSeek models. SGLang also supports MLA. The kernel choice changes the KV cache FORMAT: FlashMLA uses 528 bytes/token for FP8 (512 bytes e4m3 + 16 bytes e8m0 scales) or 288 bytes/token for FP4 (256 bytes e2m1 + 32 bytes e4m3 scales). This is a hard constraint: a kernel that hard-codes the KV format will not accept another engine's cache.
scales_with: context_length (KV cache bytes scale linearly)
kv_cache_dtype (fp8/fp4/bf16 - FlashMLA only supports fp8/fp4)
num_layers (MLA cache per layer is (d_c+d_rh) elements)
head_dim (d_c = kv_lora_rank, typically 512)

flop_classes.name: Paged attention block-size constraints: kernels that hard-code block size and the compression ratio trap
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: PagedAttention (vLLM) manages KV cache in fixed-size blocks. The block size is a kernel constraint, not just a storage choice. FlashAttention's paged path requires page_block_size to be a multiple of 256. Some kernels hard-code the block size entirely, so a different compression ratio has no solution. The block_table is per (batch, max_num_blocks_per_seq) int32. Paging changes no arithmetic - FLOPs and total bytes are identical. What changes is coalescing efficiency and the absence of per-request reallocation copies. The real payoff is capacity (no wasted padding) and elimination of defragmentation copies. vLLM achieves near-zero waste in KV cache memory and 2-4x throughput improvement vs FasterTransformer and Orca.
scales_with: context_length
batch_size
page size (must be multiple of 256 in FA-2 paged path)
num_kv_heads

flop_classes.name: Attention kernel regime map: what wins at each context length and batch size
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The optimal attention kernel depends on context length, batch size, and hardware. SHORT CONTEXT (L < 4K), SMALL BATCH (B < 8): FA-2 or FA-3 with standard tiling. The kernel is compute-bound; tiling efficiency is high. FA-2 achieves 50-73% peak on A100. FA-3 achieves 75% on H100. SHORT CONTEXT, LARGE BATCH (B > 32): FA-2/FA-3 with split-KV (FlashDecoding). The KV cache is small but batch is large, so split-KV increases parallelism. FlashInfer's load-balanced scheduling adjusts to dynamic batch sizes. MEDIUM CONTEXT (4K < L < 32K), ANY BATCH: FA-3 on Hopper (warp specialization + TMA), FA-4 on Blackwell (tcgen05 + TMEM). FA-3: 740 TFLOPs/s FP16, 1.2 PFLOPs/s FP8. FA-4: 1605 TFLOPs/s BF16 on B200. LONG CONTEXT (32K < L < 128K), SMALL BATCH: FA-3/FA-4 with split-KV and paged attention. The KV cache is large; split-KV is essential for SM utilization. FlashInfer: 28-30% latency reduction for long-context. LONG CONTEXT, LARGE BATCH: MLA (DeepSeek) or sliding-window hybrid (Gemma 3). MLA reduces cache 85x, making long context feasible. Sliding-window reduces prefill cost 5.9x at 128K. VERY LONG CONTEXT (L > 128K): MLA with fp8/fp4 KV cache (FlashMLA on Blackwell). MLA cache at 128K: 68.6 KiB/token * 128K = 8.6 GiB per sequence. With fp8: 4.3 GiB. With fp4: 2.4 GiB. MHA equivalent: 5.856 MiB/token * 128K = 732 GiB - infeasible. BATCH SIZE EFFECT: at batch 1, decode attention is memory-bound with low SM utilization; split-KV is essential. At batch 32+, the GEMM is large enough to saturate SMs; split-KV is unnecessary. At batch 256+, the KV cache is large; paged attention and MLA become critical.
scales_with: context_length (determines tiling efficiency and cache size)
batch_size (determines SM utilization and split-KV necessity)
head_dim (FA-3/4 tuned for 128/256)
precision (fp8 doubles tensor-core flops but SFU exp unchanged)

flop_classes.name: SageAttention is research-only: absent from vLLM and SGLang LLM serving paths
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: SageAttention is a quantization-based attention optimization that is NOT deployed in production engines. It is absent from the vLLM source tree and in SGLang it appears only under multimodal_gen, not the LLM serving path. SageAttention quantizes attention computations to int8/fp8 to reduce compute cost, but it is research-only. The key distinction: SageAttention is not in vLLM (absent from the tree), not in SGLang's LLM path (only in multimodal_gen), and not in any production serving engine. This is a verified fact from source code inspection, not a README claim.
scales_with: context_length
batch_size
precision (int8/fp8 quantization)

flop_classes.name: Sliding-window and SSM hybrid decode: the fixed per-sequence state cost invisible in KV-per-token calculations
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Hybrid attention-SSM models have a per-sequence cost that does NOT show up in a KV-per-token calculation. For SSM layers (Mamba, etc.), the recurrent state is fixed-size per sequence: state = d_inner * N elements, where d_inner = expand * hidden and N = ssm_state_size. This state is CONSTANT in context length - it does not grow with L. For Nemotron-H-8B (hidden 4096, expand 2, N=128): state = 8192*128 = 1,048,576 elements = 2.0 MiB per layer at bf16. With 48 Mamba layers: 96.0 MiB per sequence, independent of context. Compare: 4 attention layers with 8 KV heads, head_dim 128: 4*2*8*128*2 = 16,384 bytes/token = 16 KiB/token, which at 8k context is 128 MiB and already exceeds the entire recurrent state. At 128k it is 2.0 GiB. The state is NOT free - it is a fixed per-sequence tax that stops amortising as batch grows. At batch 256, a hybrid pays 256*96 MiB = 24.6 GiB of state whether sequences are 1k or 128k tokens. This is the opposite trade from KV cache, which grows with context.
scales_with: batch_size (state is per sequence, does NOT amortise with batch)
context_length (NOT at all for SSM layers - this is the defining property)
ssm_state_size N
expand ratio (d_inner = expand*hidden)
num_mamba_layers

flop_classes.name: Sparse and structured attention variants: NSA, DSA, and their honest deployment status
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Sparse attention reduces the WORK SET but adds a full-context index pass and non-contiguous gather. NSA (Native Sparse Attention): three paths per query - compressed coarse tokens, top-k selected fine tokens, sliding window. Per-query decode work falls from L to (compressed_count + selected_count + w) while the index pass still touches all L. NSA reports 11.6x decode / 9.0x forward / 6.0x backward speedups at 64k context. But NSA names the trap: token-granular selection 'leads to the need to load a large number of individual tokens from the KV cache during attention computation. This non-contiguous memory access prevents efficient adaptation of fast attention techniques.' DSA (DeepSeek Sparse Attention, DeepSeek-V3.2): FP8-capable ReLU indexer scores every KV token, then only top-2048 are attended. Instantiated on MLA mode. The indexer is itself an attention-shaped pass over the full context. DSA's saving is a subtraction from the full-context, not a complexity class change.
scales_with: context_length (the axis every variant attacks)
sparse selection granularity (block-granular is hardware-friendly; token-granular is not)
local:global or sparse:dense ratio
indexer cost (full-context scoring pass)

flop_classes.name: Block-scaled FP8/FP4 tensor cores: MXFP and NVFP formats inside the MMA instruction
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: This is the mechanism by which precision reduction becomes FLOPs rather than a dequantization tax. From the PTX ISA shape tables: warp-level mma has .e4m3/.e5m2 at .m16n8k32 (PTX 8.4) and .m16n8k16 (8.7); .e3m2/.e2m3/.e2m1 at .m16n8k32 (8.7); and BLOCK-SCALED forms where the multiplicand type is .e4m3/.e5m2/.e3m2/.e2m3/.e2m1 times a .ue8m0 scale at .m16n8k32, and .e2m1 times (.ue8m0 or .ue4m3) at .m16n8k64 (8.7). The key point: the scale is part of the MMA OPERAND, not a separate kernel, so a 32-element scale block is applied inside the tensor-core pipeline and the activation quantization no longer needs a fused dequant pass. wgmma mirrors this at warpgroup level - fp8 at .m64nNk32. tcgen05 goes further with distinct .kind values (f16, f8f6f4, mxf8f6f4, mxf4, mxf4nvf4, tf32, i8, ti16) plus .decompress::lut::b and .collector::b::* qualifiers, and CUTLASS lists higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) MMA instructions for Blackwell. The arithmetic win is the FLOP-per-byte ratio: at fp8 the tensor-core rate doubles (H100: 989 -> 1978 TFLOPS) and at fp4 it doubles again, but the SFU exponential rate does NOT change - which is precisely why FA-3 and FA-4 both had to solve the softmax bottleneck separately.
scales_with: scale block size (16/32-element blocks for ue8m0 vs ue4m3)
precision (fp8 -> fp4 doubles then quadruples tensor-core throughput)
architecture generation (wmma-level vs wgmma-level vs tcgen05 .kind)

flop_classes.name: Blackwell-specific failure modes, numerical issues, and kernel availability gaps
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Several Blackwell-specific failure modes and gaps are documented. (1) SM100 vs SM120 incompatibility: CUTLASS README explicitly warns that sm_100a-compiled kernels are NOT compatible with RTX 50 series (SM120) because SM120 has a different compute capability from datacenter SM100. This means datacenter Blackwell kernels cannot be used on consumer Blackwell GPUs and vice versa. (2) K=96 block-scaled FP4 requires sm_103a or sm_107a (not sm_100a): the tcgen05.mma .kind::mxf4/.kind::mxf4nvf4 with K=96 is only supported on sm_103a and sm_107a, not on sm_100a (B200). K=128/192 requires sm_107f or higher. This means B200 cannot use the largest block-scaled FP4 tile sizes. (3) Sub-byte types not supported for .shared::cluster.global on sm_120a: this constrains a cluster-mapped FP4 pipeline on consumer Blackwell. (4) FlashMLA removed Hopper support: the 2026.09.30 release requires NVIDIA SM100/SM103 with CUDA >= 13.1 and removed Hopper support (V3/V3.2/V4.0), so a Hopper part gets an older FlashMLA or a different MLA path entirely. (5) DeepGEMM scale format change: SM100 requires packed UE8M0 scales (four per int) while SM90 wants FP32 scales - switching an FP8 model from H100 to B200 changes the memory layout the engine must produce. (6) NVFP4 accuracy on small models: the NVFP4 blog notes 'lower risk of noticeable accuracy drop particularly for larger models' - small models may see more accuracy degradation with NVFP4. (7) Blackwell Ultra datasheet INT8 inconsistency: the Blackwell Ultra datasheet prints INT8 as '330 TOPS / 307 TOPS' which is internally inconsistent with the FP8 row (10 PFLOPS = 10,000 TOPS) by ~30x - treated as a transcription artifact. (8) The Blackwell Ultra FP4 row uses a different sparse/dense convention (Sparse|Dense) than every other row (sparse with dense=half), creating a documentation trap.
scales_with: architecture target (sm_100a vs sm_103a vs sm_107a vs sm_107f vs sm_120)
kernel library version (CUTLASS, FlashMLA, DeepGEMM)
precision format (FP4, FP8, NVFP4, MXFP4)
model size (NVFP4 accuracy varies with model size)

flop_classes.name: FP8 fine-grained scaling on Hopper vs Blackwell: per-tensor vs per-block scales and accuracy implications
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) was introduced on Hopper with per-tensor scaling: a single FP32 scale factor for the entire tensor, applied before the FP8 GEMM and after in the epilogue. This coarse scaling is problematic for tensors with high dynamic range or outliers, as a single scale cannot adequately represent both large and small values. Blackwell extends FP8 support with block-scaled formats: MXFP8 (E4M13 + UE8M0 scale per 32-value block) and NVFP8 (E4M3 + E4M3 scale per 16-value block + per-tensor FP32 scale). The tcgen05.mma instruction supports these via .kind::mxf8f6f4 (block-scaled FP8/FP6 with UE8M0 scale). The finer-grained scaling (per-16 or per-32 values instead of per-tensor) reduces quantization error by allowing different scale factors for different regions of the tensor. The accuracy implication: block-scaled FP8 can achieve close to FP16/BF16 accuracy, while per-tensor FP8 may suffer noticeable degradation on tensors with outliers. The CUTLASS block-scaled tensor core record notes that DeepGEMM requires packed UE8M0 scales (four per int) on SM100, while SM90 wants FP32 scales - this changes the memory layout the engine must produce. The existing block-scaled-tensor-core-fp4-fp8 record covers the PTX ISA shape tables; this record focuses on the Hopper-to-Blackwell evolution of FP8 scaling granularity and its accuracy implications.
scales_with: scaling granularity (per-tensor vs per-32 vs per-16)
tensor dynamic range (outliers require finer scaling)
block size (16 vs 32 values per scale)

flop_classes.name: NVFP4 and MXFP4 block-scaled formats on Blackwell: microscaling block size, per-block scales, and kernel consumption
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Blackwell supports three 4-bit floating-point formats with different block-scaling strategies. (1) FP4 (E2M1): 4 bits per value (1 sign, 2 exponent, 1 mantissa), no hardware scaling - requires software-managed scales. (2) MXFP4: E2M1 + 1 shared power-of-two scale (UE8M0) per 32-value block. Hardware-accelerated scaling. (3) NVFP4: E2M1 + 1 shared FP8 (E4M3) scale per 16-value micro-block + per-tensor FP32 scale. Hardware-accelerated scaling. The key difference: NVFP4 uses a 16-value block with FP8 E4M3 scale (non-power-of-two, fractional precision), while MXFP4 uses a 32-value block with UE8M0 scale (power-of-two only). NVFP4's finer-grained scaling (16 vs 32 values per block) and higher-precision scale (E4M3 vs UE8M0) reduce quantization error. The tcgen05.mma instruction consumes these formats via .kind::mxf4 (MXFP4 with UE8M0), .kind::mxf4nvf4 (NVFP4 with UE8M0/UE4M3/UE5M3 scales), and .kind::f8f6f4 (non-block-scaled FP4 E2M1). NVFP4 reduces model memory footprint by ~3.5x vs FP16 and ~1.8x vs FP8. Accuracy: NVFP4 achieves 1% or less degradation vs FP8 on DeepSeek-R1-0528 benchmarks. The NVFP4 pretraining recipe (arXiv 2509.25149) combines micro-block scaling, E4M3 scale factors, Hadamard transforms, selective 2D block-based quantization, and stochastic rounding. Energy efficiency: up to 25x (Blackwell) and 50x (Blackwell Ultra) vs H100 for NVFP4 workloads. The per-tensor FP32 scale in NVFP4 is computed as s_global = global_amax / (448 * 6) where 448 is the E4M3 max and 6 is the E2M1 max.
scales_with: block size (16 for NVFP4, 32 for MXFP4)
scale precision (E4M3 for NVFP4, UE8M0 for MXFP4)
model size (larger models benefit more from NVFP4's finer scaling)
quantization method (PTQ vs QAT vs pretraining recipe)

flop_classes.name: NVLink 5 and GB200/GB300 NVL72 domain topology: 72-GPU domain and crossing it
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: NVLink 5 provides 1.8 TB/s bidirectional bandwidth per GPU (vs 900 GB/s on Hopper NVLink 4), which is 14x PCIe Gen5. The GB200 NVL72 connects 72 Blackwell GPUs in a single NVLink domain using 9 NVLink switch trays, each with 144 NVLink ports at 100 GB/s, delivering 130 TB/s total NVLink bandwidth. The domain acts as a single massive GPU with 30 TB unified memory. Fifth-gen NVLink scales to 576 GPUs in a single domain with over 1 PB/s total bandwidth. The NVLink Switch Chip enables 4x bandwidth efficiency with NVIDIA SHARP (Scalable Hierarchical Aggregation and Reduction Protocol) FP8 support. What breaks when you cross the 72-GPU domain: communication falls back to InfiniBand or Ethernet, which has much higher latency and lower bandwidth. The GB200 NVL72 delivers 30x faster real-time LLM inference vs H100 (1.8T parameter GPT-MoE, TTL=50ms, FTL=5s, 32768 input/1024 output) - this requires the full 72-GPU domain. The GB200 compute tray has 2 Grace CPUs + 4 Blackwell GPUs with NVLink-C2C at 900 GB/s for coherent CPU-GPU memory access. NVLink 5 per-GPU bandwidth is a bidirectional aggregate (not per-lane per-direction). The NVL72 system uses liquid cooling and copper cable cartridges for operational simplicity.
scales_with: number of GPUs in the NVLink domain (72 for NVL72, up to 576 for full NVLink 5)
model size (larger models need more GPUs in the domain)
tensor-parallel degree (must fit within the domain for full NVLink bandwidth)
MoE expert parallelism (benefits from large domain for all-to-all communication)

flop_classes.name: Draft-model/speculative decoding support on Blackwell
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Speculative decoding on Blackwell follows the same bandwidth-trade principle as on Hopper: the draft pass reads the draft model's weights for k tokens at once, giving AI ~k flop/byte, and is memory-bound exactly like decode_gemm at effective batch k. Blackwell's advantages for speculative decoding: (1) The 5th-gen Tensor Core's higher throughput (2500 TFLOPS BF16 dense vs 989 on H100) means the verification pass (which runs the target model on k+1 tokens) is faster, but the draft pass is still memory-bound so the speedup ratio is roughly unchanged. (2) NVLink 5's 1.8 TB/s per-GPU bandwidth in GB200/GB300 NVL72 means the KV cache transfer between draft and target models (if colocated) is faster. (3) The larger HBM3e capacity (186 GB on B200, 279 GB on B300) means both models plus KV cache can be co-resident more easily. (4) FP4/NVFP4 support means the draft model can be quantized to 4-bit, reducing its memory footprint and making the draft pass cheaper. The design condition remains: the draft's per-step latency must stay below the target model's single-token latency. The speedup is bounded by (1 + draft_cost/target_cost) and by the acceptance rate. On Blackwell, the verification pass benefits from tcgen05.mma's higher throughput, but the draft pass remains memory-bound, so the overall speedup is primarily determined by the acceptance rate and the draft model's size relative to the target.
scales_with: draft_k (number of speculative positions)
draft_model_size (relative to target model)
acceptance rate (determines effective speedup)
KV cache size (must fit in HBM alongside both models)

flop_classes.name: tcgen05 5th-gen Tensor Core: native FP4/FP6 support and emulation paths
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The tcgen05.mma instruction on Blackwell (sm_100a) supports multiple .kind values that determine which precision formats are natively executed. From the PTX ISA 9.4 Table 48: .kind::f16 supports FP16/BF16 at K=16 (dense) or K=32 (sparse); .kind::f8f6f4 supports FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) and FP6 (E2M3/E3M2) at K=32 (dense) or K=64/128 (sparse), with FP4 (E2M1) at K=64 (dense) or K=128 (sparse) - but only E4M3/E5m2 for K=64; .kind::mxf8f6f4 supports block-scaled FP8/FP6 with UE8M0 scale at K=32/64 (dense) or K=64/128 (sparse); .kind::mxf4 supports block-scaled FP4 (E2M1) with UE8M0 scale at K=64/96 (dense) or K=128/192 (sparse); .kind::mxf4nvf4 supports NVFP4 (E2M1) with UE8M0/UE4M3/UE5M3 scales at K=64/96 (dense) or K=128/192 (sparse). The key distinction: FP4 E2M1 is natively supported in .kind::f8f6f4 (non-block-scaled), .kind::mxf4 (block-scaled with UE8M0), and .kind::mxf4nvf4 (NVFP4 with UE4M3/UE5M3 scales). FP6 E2M3/E3M2 is natively supported in .kind::f8f6f4 and .kind::mxf8f6f4. However, K=96 for .kind::mxf4/.kind::mxf4nvf4 is only supported on sm_103a and sm_107a (not sm_100a), and K=128/192 for those kinds requires sm_107f or higher. On sm_100a (B200), the maximum K for block-scaled FP4 is 64 (dense) or 128 (sparse). CUTLASS 4.8 lists higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) Tensor Core MMA instructions for Blackwell. The emulation path: CUTLASS example 78_blackwell_emulated_bf16x9_gemm shows FP32 emulation via BF16 on Blackwell, and example 84_blackwell_narrow_precision_sparse_gemm shows block-scaled sparse GEMM.
scales_with: precision (FP16 -> FP8 -> FP6 -> FP4 changes MMA_K and throughput)
block scaling format (none vs UE8M0 vs UE4M3/UE5M3)
architecture target (sm_100a vs sm_103a vs sm_107a vs sm_107f)
CTA group size (1 or 2 for tcgen05)

flop_classes.name: TMA + tcgen05 MMA with async copy and warp-specialization in CUTLASS Blackwell kernels
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Blackwell kernels use TMA (cp.async.bulk.tensor) for global->shared memory copies and tcgen05.mma for tensor-core operations, with warp specialization to overlap data movement with compute. The producer-consumer pattern: producer warps issue TMA copies (cp.async.bulk.tensor) to move tiles from HBM to shared memory, while consumer warps issue tcgen05.mma instructions to perform matrix multiplications. This is the Blackwell analogue of Hopper's FA-3 warp specialization (producer warps issue TMA, consumer warps issue WGMMA). The key difference: tcgen05.mma is issued by a single thread (not a warpgroup), accumulates in TMEM (not registers), and can span 2 CTAs. TMA on Blackwell supports .multicast::cluster::32b qualifier for tcgen05.commit and mbarrier.expect_tx (PTX ISA 9.4), enabling multicast completion. The .shared::cluster.global direction is 'optimized for' sm_90a/sm_100a/sm_100f/sm_103a/sm_103f/sm_107a/sm_107f/sm_110a/sm_110f. CUTLASS 3.x on Blackwell SM100 uses umma/tcgen05 instructions. CUTLASS 4.8 adds CuTe DSL support for Blackwell with FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) Tensor Core MMA instructions. The async copy pipeline: TMA does address generation and bounds predication in hardware, freeing registers so tiles can be larger. Larger tiles amortize each HBM byte over more MACs. The tcgen05.mma accumulator in TMEM means the MMA pipeline does not compete with CUDA-core work for registers, enabling deeper pipelining.
scales_with: tile size (larger tiles = more FLOPs per HBM byte)
number of pipeline stages (TMEM capacity limits accumulator count)
warp specialization granularity (producer vs consumer warp count)
CTA group size (1 or 2 for tcgen05)

flop_classes.name: Chunked prefill and prefill/decode interleaving: deciding when to interrupt a prefill for a decode step
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Not an arithmetic mechanism; it is the knob that decides the arithmetic-intensity mix of a step. A full prefill step has AI ~ prompt_length (large-M GEMM, compute-bound); a decode step has AI = batch (memory-bound). Chunked prefill splits a long prompt into chunks of `max_num_batched_tokens` and admits at most one chunk per scheduler iteration, so the prefill's compute-rich contribution to a step is bounded, and decode iterations interleave between chunks. That is the point: a step that is mostly prefill chunk plus decode rows has a higher average AI than a pure decode step, which converts idle bandwidth into tokens, but it also has per-iteration shape variation that fights CUDA Graphs' static-configuration requirement. SARATHI's framing is the same lever stated differently - piggybacking decodes onto chunked prefills rather than giving them their own iteration.
scales_with: max_num_batched_tokens (the chunk size - the direct knob on how much prefill can be admitted into one step)
prompt_length (how many chunks a request needs, and therefore how many decode iterations it waits behind)
batch_size (decode rows riding along with the chunk)
scheduler_priority_policy (prefill-first starves decode ITL; decode-first inflates TTFT)
num_concurrent_requests (arrival pressure determines whether chunking or full-prefill admission dominates)

flop_classes.name: On PCIe-attached gfx906, the cross-GPU all-reduce in decode is interconnect-bound and makes decode throughput decline as GPUs are added
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Extremely low at batch 1 decode: each added GPU adds a full activation all-reduce over PCIe while contributing only its share of a weight-streaming GEMV. MI50 moves ~1 TB/s of weights per card, so per-GPU weight traffic is the term that shrinks with added GPUs while the all-reduce term does not.
scales_with: num_gpus
tensor_parallel_size
context_length
expert_parallel_groups

flop_classes.name: Grammar-mask evaluation per token in constrained / structured decoding
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Grammar-mask evaluation is a per-token cost incurred AFTER the logits exist, and it scales with vocabulary size rather than with model size. A naive CFG-constrained decoder, as the XGrammar paper's abstract describes it, 'requires going through several stack states over all tokens in vocabulary during runtime, bringing non-negligible overhead for structured generation' - note that 'over all tokens in vocabulary' is the whole cost model: the work is O(stack_depth * V) per token. The bitmask formulation that efficient implementations use compresses that to V bits = V/8 bytes: for V = 128,256 that is 15.66 KiB per token, written once and read once by the sampler = 31.31 KiB of traffic. Against a Llama-3-8B decode step that reads 2*P = 16.06 GB of weights, the mask is 0.0002% of the step's HBM traffic, and even the O(stack_depth * V) naive form with depth 4 is about 0.0004%. So the answer to 'why is it usually not the bottleneck' is quantitative, not hand-waving: in a memory-bound decode step the weight read is 4 to 5 orders of magnitude larger than the mask. The regime where it IS the bottleneck is narrow and worth naming precisely: (a) SMALL models, where 2*P is small and V is not proportionally smaller - e.g. a sub-1B model with a 32k vocab reads only ~2 GB of weights, bringing the mask to ~0.002%, still small, so this is a weak case; (b) CPU-bound or launch-overhead-bound decoding, where an extra kernel launch per token costs more microseconds than the mask costs bytes - the kernel COUNT is the risk, not the mask size; (c) engines that run the mask on the CPU in Python, where per-token interpreter overhead is milliseconds rather than bytes.
scales_with: vocab_size V (the entire cost model is O(depth*V) naive or O(V/8) bytes as a bitmask: 15.66 KiB/token at V=128256, 3.9 KiB at V=32000)
grammar_stack_depth (the naive form's multiplier; a deeply nested JSON schema or a deeply nested tool-call grammar makes this worse)
kernel_launch_count (a mask kernel ADDED to an already launch-bound decode step is the real risk - see custom-kernel-launch-overhead)
whether the mask runs on GPU or CPU (CPU execution in Python turns a 15 KiB byte operation into a millisecond-scale host operation)
model_size (INVERSE: the mask share of a step falls as the model grows, so the risk is highest for small models and lowest for frontier ones)
output_structure (JSON with shallow nesting, versus a deeply nested grammar or many alternation branches, directly sets the number of stack states visited)

incremental-vs-full recomputation (the incremental case advances a persistent stack and copies it per live parse stack - cost scales with num_grammar_stacks = number of concurrently constrained requests, NOT with vocab; the full-recompute case this record originally described is O(depth*V) per token)

trigger_patterns and trigger_buffer length (llama.cpp re-runs every trigger_pattern.find() against the whole accumulated trigger_buffer each token while awaiting a trigger - O(tokens_so_far x num_patterns) over the response, a per-token cost that grows with output length)

whether the grammar engine is on device or host (an on-device bitmask engine with a persistent stack is O(V/8) bytes and graphable; a host-side stack machine is per-token host work that cannot be captured in a CUDA graph - see custom-kernel-launch-overhead and detokenization-stop-string-scan)

flop_classes.name: Iteration-level scheduling: the overlap of prefill and decode in one batch
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Not a flop class in isolation - it is the class that decides which flop classes a step contains. Orca's iteration-level scheduling admits a new request as soon as any sequence in the running batch finishes, so the batch never sits at one sequence and the decode GEMM's AI (= B) actually climbs. In a naive static batch, a step is either prefill-dominated (compute-bound, long TTFT) or decode-dominated (memory-bound, low per-token throughput) and neither uses the machine well. Mixing them is the point: prefill tokens are compute-rich and raise AI for the step's GEMMs, while the KV bytes the decode rows pull keep the step bandwidth-heavy. The cost is that a mixed step's shapes vary per iteration, which is exactly what fights CUDA Graphs' static-configuration requirement.
scales_with: batch_size (the lever that makes continuous batching worth having)
arrival_rate_and_sequence_length_distribution (whether steps are prefill- or decode-dominated)
num_concurrent_requests (throughput mode vs latency mode)
scheduler_policy (prefill-first vs decode-first vs chunked-prefill preemption changes the mix)
kv_cache_pressure (preemption and swapping add kv_transfer work to a step)

flop_classes.name: Cross-encoder reranking: N independent bidirectional forwards, compute-bound at batch 1
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Reranking N passages is N INDEPENDENT forward passes with no KV-cache reuse, so it is prefill-shaped and compute-bound even at batch 1 - the exact opposite of the generative decode regime. Arithmetic: for a bidirectional encoder of P parameters run over one sequence of t tokens, flops = 2*P*t while bytes = 2*P (weights read ONCE for all t rows) plus activation traffic. The per-forward AI from weights alone is therefore ~t flop/byte, i.e. t times HIGHER than the ~1 flop/byte of a decode GEMM, because the weight read is amortized across t rows instead of 1. Worked example with BERT-base geometry (d=768, 3072 intermediate, 12 layers, 12 heads x 64 head_dim), which derives to P = 12*(768*768 + 2*768*768 + 768*768 + 3*768*3072) = 12*(0.59M + 1.18M + 0.59M + 7.08M) = 12*9.44M = 113.2M against a released 110M: at the standard reranking length t = 544 tokens, flops = 2*113.2e6*544 = 123.2 GFLOP against a weight read of 2*113.2e6 = 226 MB, so AI = 544 flop/byte, which is 1.84x ABOVE H100 SXM's 295.4 ridge. Reranking is compute-bound at batch 1 - there is no memory roof to climb and no batching is required to get there. Batching N passages into one forward multiplies the amortization again: AI = N*t, so at N=64, t=544 the AI is 34,816 flop/byte, 118x the ridge, and the reranker is deep in GEMM territory. Attention is a rounding error at reranking lengths even though the mask is FULL (bidirectional, 2x the causal flops): full-mask attention flops = 2 * 2*n_q*dh*t^2 = 4*12*64*544^2 = 0.91 GFLOP against 123.2 GFLOP of GEMM = 0.7%. The attention crossover is L* = P_layer/(n_q*dh) = 9.44M/768 = 12,288 tokens, far beyond any realistic pair length - a cross-encoder is a pure GEMM machine. Corpus cost, and why this shape is worth its own record: Sentence-BERT quantifies the alternative, noting that with BERT 'finding the most similar pair in a collection of 10,000 sentences requires about 50 million inference computations (~65 hours)' - 10,000 x 10,000 = 100M pairs, each a full forward. That is N scaling linearly with corpus size, which no amount of batching can fix: batching improves AI, not total flops.
scales_with: num_passages_reranked N (flops scale LINEARLY - N independent forwards, and batching raises AI without reducing flops)
corpus_size (N is typically top-k of a first-stage retrieval, so cost is top_k times the pair length; over a full corpus it is quadratic)
pair_length t (AI = t from the weight amortization alone; this is why a reranker is compute-bound where a generator is not)
model_size (reranker flops scale with P linearly - a 300M cross-encoder costs 3x a 110M one per passage)
bidirectional_vs_causal_mask (full attention doubles attention flops vs causal, which is negligible at realistic pair lengths but doubles them at L*)
num_candidates_from_first_stage (the whole cost knob: rerank top-20 vs top-100 is a 5x difference in a bill that nothing else can reduce)

flop_classes.name: What a 128K prefill actually costs: flops, wall-clock, energy and dollars
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Prefill flops are 2*N_active*L for the weight GEMMs plus 2*n_q*d_h*L^2 for causal attention, and at 128K the FIRST term dominates for every current dense model - which is the counter-intuitive result and the one worth internalizing. Using active (not total) parameters so MoE models are priced correctly, at L = 131,072 on one H100 SXM (dense bf16 989.5 TFLOP/s from [[flop-nvidia-h100-specs]]): Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, 3B active, 786.4 TFLOP GEMM + 140.7 TFLOP attention = 15.2 percent attention, 937 ms at 100 percent of peak / 1,874 ms at 50 percent / 3,123 ms at 30 percent. Llama-3.1-8B, 8.03B active, 2,105.0 + 140.7 = 2,245.7 TFLOP, 6.3 percent attention, 2,270 / 4,539 / 7,565 ms. DeepSeek-V3, 37B active, 9,699.3 + 844.4 = 10,543.7 TFLOP, 8.0 percent attention, 10,656 / 21,311 / 35,519 ms. Qwen3-235B-A22B, 22B active, 5,767.2 + 281.5 = 6,048.7 TFLOP, 4.7 percent attention, 6,113 / 12,226 / 20,376 ms. GLM-4.5, 32B active, 8,388.6 + 422.2 = 8,810.8 TFLOP, 4.8 percent attention, 8,904 / 17,809 / 29,681 ms. Mistral-Large-2411, 123B active, 32,243.7 + 422.2 = 32,665.9 TFLOP, 1.3 percent attention, 33,013 / 66,025 / 110,042 ms. Qwen2.5-72B, 72.7B active, 19,057.9 + 281.5 = 19,339.4 TFLOP, 1.5 percent attention, 19,545 / 39,089 / 65,149 ms. Llama-3.1-70B, 70.6B active, 18,507.4 + 281.5 = 18,788.9 TFLOP, 1.5 percent attention, 18,988 / 37,976 / 63,294 ms. Llama-3.1-405B, 405.9B active, 106,404.2 + 562.9 = 106,967.1 TFLOP, 0.5 percent attention, 108,102 / 216,205 / 360,341 ms - 108 seconds of pure prefill for one prompt on one card, before any decode. THE ATTENTION SHARE ONLY LOOKS SMALL BECAUSE L IS STILL BELOW THE CROSSOVER for these geometries, and the crossover is per-model, not universal: Llama-3.1-70B's attention share is 0.04 percent at 4K, 0.4 percent at 32K, 1.5 percent at 128K and 3.0 percent at 256K, doubling per doubling of L, so a model with a narrow MLP per layer crosses much later than a wide one. DeepSeek-V3 is already past its crossover at 128K (8.0 percent attention, and its 844.4 TFLOP attention term is 6x Llama-3.1-70B's because n_q*d_h = 128*192 = 24,576 against 8,192). The load-bearing point: at 128K the O(L^2) term is NOT what makes prefill expensive - the O(L) weight-GEMM term is, and it is enormous. Prefill at long context is a tensor-core GEMM problem that happens to also run an attention kernel, which is the same conclusion the repo's [[long-context-rag-prefill]] reaches at 32K and takes further here.
scales_with: context length (linearly in total flops - so 4x the context is 4x the prefill bill, unlike the quadratic attention term which is still the minority)
active parameters per token (the linear term; this is why a 22B-active 235B MoE prefills 2.8x cheaper than a dense 70B at the same context)
attention geometry n_q*d_h (the quadratic term's coefficient, and the reason MLA-style narrow heads keep the quadratic term small)
achieved MFU (the 50 percent column is the realistic planning figure; 30 percent is a busy multi-tenant card)
tensor-parallel degree and interconnect (all flops divided, but each added card adds an all-reduce per layer)

flop_classes.name: Claimed vs effective context length per model (RULER): the advertised number and the measured one, side by side
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: This record is not an arithmetic-intensity claim; the cost side of long context lives in [[ctx-kv-cache-gib-at-claimed-context]] and [[ctx-128k-prefill-compute-cost]]. What it establishes is the input side: how much of the advertised context a model actually uses. RULER defines effective context length as the longest tested length (4K/8K/16K/32K/64K/128K) whose 13-task average score clears the threshold equal to Llama-2-7B-chat's own score at 4K, which the paper reports as 85.6 percent; passing lengths are marked by underlining in the paper's tables and restated in the Claimed/Effective columns of the repo's results table. Using one model's own short-context score as the bar is what makes the metric self-referential and comparable across model sizes: it asks 'does this model still do this task at 4K as well as a 4K model did'. AVERAGE GAP ACROSS THE MODELS MEASURED BY NVIDIA LOCALLY (claimed / effective / ratio): Yi-34B 200K/32K = 6.3x; Command-R-plus 128K/32K = 4.0x; Command-R 128K/32K = 4.0x; Qwen2-72B 128K/32K = 4.0x; Mistral-Large-2407 128K/32K = 4.0x; Mixtral-8x22B 64K/32K = 2.0x; Phi3-medium 128K/32K = 4.0x; Llama-3.1-8B 128K/32K = 4.0x; ProLong-8B 512K/32K = 16x; MegaBeam-Mistral 512K/32K = 16x; Mistral-v0.2-7B 32K/16K = 2.0x; Mistral-Nemo 128K/16K = 8x; GradientAI-Llama-3-70B-1048k 1M/16K = 64x; GradientAI-Llama-3-8B-1048k 1M/16K = 64x; InternLM2.5-7B-1M 1M/4K = 256x; GLM3-6B-128K 128K/4K = 32x; LWM-7B-Chat-1M 1M/<4K = >256x; DBRX 32K/8K = 4.0x; Qwen1.5-72B 32K/8K = 4.0x; Together-Llama-2-7B-32K 32K/4K = 8x; LongChat-7B 32K/<4K = >8x; LongAlpaca-13B 32K/<4K = >8x. MODELS THAT CLEAR 128K (no gap within the tested range): Llama-3.1-70B 128K/64K (2.0x), GPT-4-1106-preview 128K/64K (2.0x), GLM-4-9B-1M 1M/64K (>16x claimed but effective only 64K), Gemini-1.5-Pro 1M/>128K, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M 1M/>128K, Qwen3-235B-A22B 128K/>128K, Qwen3-14B 128K/>128K, Jamba-1.5-large 256K/>128K, Jamba-1.5-mini 256K/>128K. THE GAP SHRINKS FAST WITH MODEL SIZE, which is the single most actionable pattern in the table: within one family at one context claim, Llama-3.1-70B reaches 64K where Llama-3.1-8B reaches 32K; GLM-4-9B-1M reaches 64K where GLM3-6B-128K reaches 4K; Yi's own ablation holds training length and data blend fixed across 6B/9B/34B at 200K and finds effective length rises with size; Qwen3-30B-A3B (30B) reaches only 64K while Qwen3-32B (32B dense) clears 128K, and Qwen3-8B reaches 64K. So 'the context window does not work' is usually 'the context window does not work at this parameter count'. Where the gap is worst is the fine-tune-on-top-of-a-frozen-base family: LongChat-7B <4K, LongAlpaca-13B <4K, Together-32K 4K, DBRX 8K, GradientAI-1048k 16K - all fine-tuned continuations whose claimed length is several times the length they were actually trained at. Also note the two AGGREGATE metrics RULER reports, which disagree with each other and both disagree with the effective length: a linearly-increasing weighted average (inc) that assumes short contexts dominate real traffic, and a decreasing one (dec) that assumes long ones do. Llama-3.1-70B scores 89.6 avg / 85.5 wAvg-inc / 93.7 wAvg-dec, and Command-R-plus-0824 87.9 / 83.4 / 92.4 - so which aggregate you read decides whether Command-R-plus looks better or worse than Llama-3.1-70B. Effective length is the metric that survives both, because it is a threshold crossing rather than an average.
scales_with: parameter count (larger models hold effective length longer - the dominant observed effect)
how the context was obtained (fine-tuning a short-context base underperforms pre-training at length, per RULER's own ablation)
position-embedding scaling method, which is only half the story and is recorded separately in [[ctx-rope-scaling-method-per-model]]
task category (multi-hop tracing collapses first; see the per-category table in notes)

flop_classes.name: FP8 KV cache: 2x concurrency at 128K, and why it fails differently at long context than at short
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: KV-cache dtype is the cleanest 2x in the whole stack: bytes per cached token halve from bf16's 2 bytes/element to fp8_e4m3's 1, so decode attention - which the repo already derives as memory-bound at AI = g (the GQA group ratio) flop/byte, independent of both batch and context length - reads half the bytes at the same flops, and decode AI doubles from g to 2g. Every consequence in this record follows from that one halving plus one non-arithmetic fact: with fp8 KV, vLLM's --kv-cache-dtype fp8 runs the ENTIRE attention computation (QK and ScoreV matmuls, and queries too under FA3) in the FP8 domain rather than only storing the cache compressed. That is a much bigger change than 'store the cache smaller' and it is where the long-context-specific failure lives. THE HOPPER ACCUMULATION BUG, which is the concrete long-context-specific degradation and the reason this record exists. Hopper's FP8 tensor cores are documented as accumulating into FP32 registers, but in practice the intermediate accumulation loses precision once the CONTRACTION DIMENSION is large. In the Softmax(AttnScore)*V matmul during long-context inference, the contraction dimension IS the context length. The measured consequence: on a 128k needle-in-a-haystack task, FP8 KV scored 13 percent against a 91 percent BF16 baseline - a 78-point collapse, with no error, no warning, and no change in the latency histogram. vLLM traced it to imprecise FP32 accumulation in the tensor cores, noting this is a known hardware-level issue also hit during DeepSeek-V3 training. The fix is two-level accumulation (flash-attention PR #104, following SageAttention2, arXiv 2411.10958), which writes partially accumulated results into a real FP32 register and brought 128k NIAH from 13 percent back to 89 percent. The trigger is explicit: the failure appears when the contraction dimension reaches 100K or more. SO THE DEGRADATION IS LENGTH-DEPENDENT BY CONSTRUCTION - this is the answer to 'does KV quantization degrade differently at long context than short'. It is not a smooth precision curve; there is a cliff at roughly 100K tokens that exists because of an arithmetic property of the matmul, and a workload at 8K or 32K cannot exhibit it no matter how badly its scales are chosen. The cost of the fix is prefill, not decode: two-level accumulation raises register pressure, and on gemma-4-E2B (head_dim 256) the TTFT quadratic coefficient rose from 6.93e-07 to 1.12e-06 ms/token^2, about 1.6x slower prefill. On head_dim 64 and 128 the optimized tile sizes recover most of that; on head_dim 256 the blog states prefill remains behind BF16. ON BLACKWELL THE BUG DOES NOT EXIST: on B200 with FlashInfer the accumulation issue is fixed and no two-level accumulation is needed - a hardware-generation difference in whether long-context FP8 attention is safe out of the box.
scales_with: context length (bytes per token halve, but the accumulation-precision failure turns on at ~100K contraction length, so the error term is a step function of L)
head_dim (256 pays ~1.6x prefill from two-level accumulation; 64 and 128 mostly do not)
whether layers are full-attention or sliding-window (small windows cannot amortize the overhead - skip them)
attention backend (FA3 on Hopper needs two-level accumulation; FlashInfer on B200 does not; FlashMLA on MLA models is a third, less-validated path)
tensor-parallel degree (cache shards, so the 2x capacity win applies per card)

flop_classes.name: KV cache at the claimed context length, and how many 128K-context users one H100 or H200 can actually serve
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: KV bytes per token is exact arithmetic with no measurement in it: B_per_token = n_attn_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * 2 (K and V) * bytes_per_element, with bytes_per_element = 2 for bf16, 1 for fp8_e4m3 or int8, 0.5 for fp4. Two cases need care. MLA does not use that formula: DeepSeek V2/V3/V3.2 and Kimi-K2 store a latent cache of kv_lora_rank 512 + qk_rope_head_dim 64 = 576 elements per layer, so B_per_token = n_layers * 576 * bytes_per_element = 61*576*2 = 70,272 B = 68.6 KiB, and there is no num_key_value_heads term at all - num_key_value_heads is 128 in the config and irrelevant to cache size. Qwen3-Next is a hybrid: full_attention_interval 4 over 48 layers means 12 attention layers and 36 gated-deltanet linear-attention layers, so only 12 layers contribute KV: 12 * 2 * 256 * 2 * 2 = 24,576 B = 24.0 KiB per token, the cheapest full-attention cache in this set. Everything else in the table is dense GQA or MQA and uses the first formula. BYTES PER TOKEN AND THE TWO LENGTHS THAT MATTER (all bf16, computed from config.json in [[ctx-src-hf-configs-longctx-models]]): Llama-3.1-8B 131,072 B/tok = 128.0 KiB, 16.00 GiB at 128K, 122.07 GiB at 1M. Llama-3.1-70B 327,680 B = 320.0 KiB, 40.00 GiB at 128K, 305.18 GiB at 1M. Llama-3.1-405B 516,096 B = 504.0 KiB, 63.00 GiB at 128K, 480.65 GiB at 1M. Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M (identical geometry) 57,344 B = 56.0 KiB, 7.00 GiB at 128K, 53.41 GiB at 1M. Qwen2.5-72B 327,680 B = 320.0 KiB, 40.00 GiB at 128K. Qwen3-8B 147,456 B = 144.0 KiB, 18.00 GiB at 128K, 137.33 GiB at 1M. Qwen3-235B-A22B 192,512 B = 188.0 KiB, 23.50 GiB at 128K, 179.29 GiB at 1M. Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B 24,576 B = 24.0 KiB, 3.00 GiB at 128K, 22.89 GiB at 1M. Mistral-Large-2411 360,448 B = 352.0 KiB, 44.00 GiB at 128K, 335.69 GiB at 1M. Command-R-plus-0824 262,144 B = 256.0 KiB, 32.00 GiB at 128K, 244.14 GiB at 1M. Yi-34B-200K 245,760 B = 240.0 KiB, 30.00 GiB at 128K, 228.88 GiB at 1M. GLM-4.9B-chat-1M 81,920 B = 80.0 KiB, 10.00 GiB at 128K, 76.29 GiB at 1M. ChatGLM3-6B-128K 32,768 B = 32.0 KiB, 4.00 GiB at 128K. GLM-4.5 376,832 B = 368.0 KiB, 46.00 GiB at 128K, 350.95 GiB at 1M. DeepSeek-V2-Chat 69,120 B = 67.5 KiB (60 layers), 8.44 GiB at 128K. DeepSeek-V3 / Kimi-K2 70,272 B = 68.6 KiB, 8.58 GiB at 128K, 4.29 GiB in fp8, 2.14 GiB in fp4. THE HEADLINE: at 128K, a 128K-token sequence's KV cache alone ranges from 3.00 GiB (Qwen3-Next hybrid) to 63.00 GiB (Llama-3.1-405B) across models a practitioner might choose for the same job - a 21x spread driven entirely by config, and a second-order effect next to how many of them fit on the card at all.
scales_with: context length (linear in tokens, and that is the whole problem: doubling context doubles the cache and halves concurrency)
num_kv_heads and head_dim and n_attn_layers (the exact product, so GQA ratio and layer count are the two levers that matter)
kv_cache_dtype (2 bytes bf16 -> 1 byte fp8/int8 -> 0.5 byte fp4; a 4x spread between bf16 and fp4)
tensor-parallel degree (the cache shards by TP, so TP buys concurrency back at the cost of per-layer all-reduce; a 70B at TP4 puts 80 KiB/token on each card instead of 320)

flop_classes.name: Which attention kernels can run long-context attention on which hardware: the SM-level gate on whether long context is servable at all
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Kernel availability at long context is a gate, not a tax: it decides whether a context length is servable on a given card, before any efficiency question is asked. The gate is the streaming-multiprocessor generation, because each FlashAttention generation needs a specific tensor-core and memory primitive that only exists on one architecture. FA-1 requires Ampere or newer (SM80 and up). FA-2 adds better Ampere and Ada scheduling but is still SM80+. FA-3 REQUIRES Hopper (SM90) - it is built on wgmma plus TMA, warp specialization and asynchronous copy, and there is no SM80 fallback path. FA-4 REQUIRES Blackwell (SM100/SM103) - it is built on tcgen05 UMMA, TMEM and 2-CTA MMA. FlashMLA is NARROWER STILL: the 2026.09.30 release requires SM100/SM103 with CUDA >= 13.1 and REMOVED Hopper support plus the V3/V3.2/V4.0 model support, so on an H100 a working FlashMLA requires an older pinned checkout. The practical consequence is that a hardware fleet is stratified by which context lengths it can serve at all: an SM80 fleet (A100, A10, L40S, RTX 4090) has FA-1/FA-2 and no fp8 tensor-core attention path with online softmax; an SM90 fleet (H100, H200) has FA-3, the best-tested fp8 KV path, but no current FlashMLA; an SM100/SM103 fleet (B200, B300, GB200/GB300 NVL72) has FA-4 and FlashMLA but the FlashMLA KV format is FP8 or FP4 ONLY - unquantized bf16 KV is explicitly not supported by FlashMLA decode. So on Blackwell the cheapest KV format and the only MLA kernel are the same choice. FlashInfer is the cross-architecture JIT path: it is used as an attention backend by both SGLang and vLLM, and on B200 it is the backend that makes fp8 KV safe without Hopper's two-level accumulation workaround - but its template instantiations do not cover every head size, and vLLM validates head_size at engine init, so forcing the FlashInfer backend on a model with head_dim 256 or 512 aborts with 'Selected backend AttentionBackendEnum.FLASHINFER is not valid for this configuration. Reason: [head_size not supported]' even though the CLI override was accepted. That last point is not cosmetic for this record: Qwen3-Next ships head_dim 256, and FP8 KV on head_dim 256 costs about 1.6x prefill from two-level accumulation - so the one architecture family whose KV cache is 21x cheaper than Llama-3.1-405B's is also the one whose flagship attention backend may refuse to start and whose fp8 prefill is slower than bf16.
scales_with: SM generation (SM80 / SM90 / SM100-103 - the gate itself)
context length (above 32K, split-KV and paged attention become essential for SM utilization; above 128K the repo's regime map says only MLA with fp8/fp4 KV is practical)
head_dim (a hard filter in FlashInfer template selection, and the multiplier on fp8 two-level-accumulation prefill cost)
kv_cache_dtype (on FlashMLA, fp8 or fp4 only; on FA-3, fp8 needs two-level accumulation on Hopper)
batch size (at batch 1 decode attention has low SM utilization and split-KV is mandatory; at batch 32+ the GEMM saturates SMs and split-KV stops paying)

flop_classes.name: Why the gap exists: which RoPE/context-extension method each long-context model actually used, and trained-at-shorter-than-licensed
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Position-embedding scaling does not change attention FLOPs or KV bytes at all - it is a pure index remap on the rotary phase. AI is unchanged; what changes is whether the model's learned function of relative distance still matches the distances it is now being asked about. That is why this record is filed under prefill_attention as a QUALIFIER on that cost rather than a cost of its own: a model whose rope settings were extended without matching training sees the same prefill bill as one that was properly trained, and produces worse answers for it. The arithmetic that does move: NTK-aware scaling and YaRN change the base theta, so effective wavelength coverage per dimension changes, and PI/LongRoPE change per-dimension position division, which resamples position indices rather than rotating them - neither adds flops, and neither adds a single byte to the KV cache, which stores post-projection K and V with no positional information in them at all. The serving consequence is therefore entirely on the accuracy side of [[ctx-claimed-vs-effective-context-table]], not the cost side.
scales_with: the extension factor (rope_scaling.factor: 8x for Llama 3.1, 40x for DeepSeek V2/V3, 32x for Kimi-K2)
the training length actually used versus the advertised length (original_max_position_embeddings vs max_position_embeddings)
base theta (500000 for Llama 3.1, 1e6 for Qwen2.5/Qwen3, 1e7 for Qwen3-Next and Yi, 10000 for DeepSeek V2/V3/V3.2, 50000 for Kimi-K2, 8e6 for Command-R-plus)

flop_classes.name: Per-kernel launch and dispatch overhead at batch 1
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Not a byte/flop quantity - it is a fixed CPU-side cost per kernel launch, measured in microseconds, paid before any bytes move. At batch 1 a decode step runs on the order of a few hundred to a few thousand kernels (attention, norms, activations, GEMMs, residuals, sampling), so launch and dispatch overhead can be a visible fraction of step latency even when the GPU work itself is only tens of microseconds. This is why CUDA Graphs exist: capture the launch sequence once, replay it, and remove per-kernel launch overhead - the mechanism engines reach for precisely when B is 1 and every op is too small to amortize its own dispatch. The consequence for scheduling is that CUDAGraph requires static shapes, which is why FlashInfer's load-balanced scheduler is designed to stay compatible with CUDAGraph's static configuration.
scales_with: batch_size (inverse - at high batch each launch amortizes over more work and this stops mattering)
num_kernels_per_layer (model depth x ops per layer)
number_of_experts (MoE dispatch launches per layer)
host CPU speed and driver overhead (this is a CPU-bound cost)
static-vs-dynamic shapes (dynamic shapes force re-capture or eager launch)

ITERATION-LEVEL scheduler CPU (a separate, larger cost from per-kernel launch: 11.7% of wall on Qwen3-0.6B / H100 / enforce_eager / num_seqs=256, measured as schedule() 7.2% + update_from_output() 4.8%)
num_scheduled_tokens per step (vLLM flags its own update_from_output loop: 'can be up to 1K or more ... can be a performance bottleneck')
enforce_eager / graph-capture state (eager paths re-enter Python per step and cannot amortise anything)

flop_classes.name: CUTLASS collective GEMM: the arch-tagged Tensor Core mainloop that most production GEMM kernels wrap
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: A GEMM at batch B is memory-bound below the ridge point and compute-bound above it; a tile-based mainloop does not change that crossover, it changes how close a real kernel gets to it. What CUTLASS's collective mainloop actually reduces is shared-memory traffic per FLOP: a tile of size BM x BN x BK re-reads each operand element once per tile traverse rather than once per output element, so HBM bytes per FLOP falls as 1/BN (for A) and 1/BM (for B). Tile size is bounded by the hardware: on Hopper the extended static shared memory is 228 KB per CTA (PTX ISA) versus the 48 KB per-CTA static default, which is what permits the large Hopper tiles; CUTLASS lists 328 KB shared-memory allocations for Blackwell-class targets. Register pressure bounds the other side - accumulator tiles live in registers (Hopper WGMMA) or in tensor memory (Blackwell tcgen05), and that choice determines how many pipeline stages fit before spilling.
scales_with: tile size (BM, BN, BK)
batch_size (M dimension)
hidden_width
precision
num_SMs

flop_classes.name: Attention over the KV cache in the decode step
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Structurally ~1 flop/byte for MHA at EVERY context length and EVERY batch size - and CONFIRMED by KIVI's abstract, which states the two-part failure independently: as batch size and context length grow the KV cache 'becomes the new bottleneck in speed and memory usage', AND separately 'the loading of the KV cache causes the computational core to be idle, which limits the inference speed'. An idle compute core is the arithmetic-intensity statement in plain words. Derivation, per decoded token, one query row, n_q query heads, n_kv KV heads, head_dim d_h, context length L, bf16 KV: flops = 2*L*d_h*n_q (QK^T) + 2*L*d_h*n_q (PV) = 4*L*d_h*n_q; bytes = 2 tensors (K and V) * L*d_h*n_kv * 2 bytes = 4*L*d_h*n_kv. AI = 4*L*d_h*n_q / (4*L*d_h*n_kv) = n_q/n_kv = g, the GQA group ratio, independent of B AND independent of L. CORRECTION to an earlier version of this field: it stated AI = 1 flop/byte unconditionally. That is true only for MHA (g=1). For Llama-3-8B (32 query / 8 KV heads) AI = 4; for Llama-2-70B (64 query / 8 KV heads) AI = 8; for MQA with 32 query heads AI = 32. The qualitative conclusion survives and is if anything strengthened - AI is a constant of the architecture, not a function of any serving knob - but the magnitude was wrong by the group ratio, and it matters because that ratio is exactly what GQA/MQA and KV-cache dtype quantization are being asked to buy. With int8/fp8 KV (1 byte per element instead of 2) bytes halve and AI doubles, so AI = 2g: Llama-3-8B goes from 4.0 to 8.0 flop/byte. Against H100 SXM's dense-bf16 ridge of 295.4 flop/byte (989.5/3350), the gap is: MHA bf16 KV 295x below; GQA-8 bf16 37x below; GQA-8 int8 18x below; and even the aggressive combination MQA with 64 query heads (g=64) at int8 KV gives AI = 128, still 2.3x below the ridge. So NO standard attention configuration reaches the compute roof, at any context length, at any batch size, at any dtype. The consequence is sharper than for prefill: because flops and bytes both scale linearly in context length, growing context does NOT raise arithmetic intensity, and batching does NOT raise it either. Continuous batching therefore gives no relief here, unlike for decode_gemm, and long-context ITL degrades linearly in L for every sequence in the batch at once - there is no batch size at which the wall recedes.
scales_with: context_length (bytes AND flops both linear - AI flat at g, so cost per token grows linearly with context with no regime change)
batch_size (bytes and flops both linear - AI flat, batching does not amortize this class at all; the sharpest structural difference from decode_gemm)
num_kv_heads / gqa group ratio g (the only knob that cuts bytes without cutting flops, and it is fixed at training time)
kv_cache_dtype (fp8/int8 KV halves bytes and doubles AI to 2g; KIVI pushes this to 2-bit with per-channel keys and per-token values)
context length against available cache (once the KV no longer fits, paging and re-computation add a kv_transfer component and degradation gets worse than linear)

flop_classes.name: Dense weight GEMMs in the decode step (the per-token matmul tax)
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: AI = B flop/byte, exactly, at batch B in bf16 - this is the definitional result and it explains most decode benchmarks. Derivation: every weight in the model is read from HBM exactly once per step and reused across all B rows, so bytes = 2*N_params (2 bytes per weight) while flops = 2*B*N_params (a multiply-add is 2 flops), giving AI = B. At batch 1 that is 1 flop/byte, i.e. a batch-1 decode GEMM sits ~295x below H100 SXM's dense-bf16 ridge point of 295.4 flop/byte and runs at a small fraction of peak purely because it is waiting on HBM. Ridge-crossing batch per part, computed as ridge = 1000*TFLOPs / GB_per_s from the accelerator records' own DENSE figures (1000*TFLOPs / GB/s = flop per byte): H100 SXM bf16 989.5/3350 = 295.4, so B_ridge = 295; H100 SXM fp8 1979/3350 = 590.7, so B_ridge = 591; MI300X bf16 1307.4/5300 = 246.7, so B_ridge = 247; MI300X fp8 2614.9/5300 = 493.4, so B_ridge = 493; RTX 4090 bf16 165.2/1008 = 163.9, so B_ridge = 164, and fp8 330.3/1008 = 327.7, so B_ridge = 328; TPU v5e bf16 197/819 = 240.5, so B_ridge = 241; A100 SXM 312/2039 = 153.0, so B_ridge = 153; B200 bf16 2500/8000 = 312.5, so B_ridge = 313. Because AI rises exactly linearly in B and the ridge is a fixed property of the part, the crossover batch is a fully determined number rather than a range to be tuned: it IS the part's ridge. Practical reading of the table: every data-center part here crosses at B of roughly 150-600 in bf16, so no single-stream serving configuration is ever compute-bound on the weight GEMMs, and the parts differ in HOW FAR below the ridge they sit at B=1 (a 4090 is 164x below, an H100 295x below) but not in whether they are. CORRECTION to an earlier version of this field: NVIDIA's H100 datasheet marks headline figures with an asterisk for sparsity, and 989.5 x 2 = 1979 shows 1979 is both the bf16 SPARSE figure and the dense fp8 figure - the two coincide, which is exactly why a dense fp8 count must be read from a field that states dense/sparse explicitly rather than inferred from the asterisk.
scales_with: batch_size (AI = B, the only lever that moves decode off the memory roof; the crossover batch equals the part's ridge)
num_params
hidden_width / intermediate_size (bytes and flops both scale with it, so AI is unchanged)
dtype (fp8 or int4 weights cut bytes directly and raise AI proportionally, doubling the tolerable batch per halving of weight bytes)
tensor_parallel_degree (sharding weights N ways divides bytes and flops by N each, leaving per-device AI at B unchanged while adding a per-layer all-reduce whose payload scales with B)

flop_classes.name: DeepEP expert-parallel dispatch/combine: an all-to-all that is itself a kernel and overlaps compute
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Not FLOPs - bytes, and specifically bytes that cross NVLink or RDMA rather than HBM. Dispatch moves each routed token's activation to the rank owning its expert; combine moves expert outputs back. The kernel-level content is the overlap: num_sms bounds how many SMs the communication kernel occupies so expert GEMMs can run concurrently, and defer_epilogue=True with async_with_compute_stream=True returns an EventOverlap so the dispatch epilogue runs on the current stream while compute proceeds. With do_cpu_sync=False (the decode path) the kernel avoids a CPU synchronization entirely, allocating outputs to configured capacity and exposing psum_num_recv_tokens_per_expert for the downstream grouped GEMM to find valid ranges - that is the difference between a decode step that stalls on a host round trip and one that does not. FP8 dispatch halves the bytes on the wire.
scales_with: num_experts and experts_per_token (total bytes moved is tokens x topk)
hidden_width
interconnect bandwidth (NVLink intranode, RDMA internode)
num_sms (communication/compute overlap budget)
expert redundancy (NVLink weight and gradient exchange for redundant experts)

flop_classes.name: DeepGEMM grouped/masked GEMM and Mega MoE: shaping MoE expert GEMMs for decode and for NVLink overlap
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Grouped GEMM changes the tiling, not the math: instead of B separate GEMMs each with a token-thin M, the tokens routed to one expert are concatenated so the expert's GEMM has a usable M dimension, which is what keeps tensor cores busy. DeepGEMM groups ONLY the M axis and requires N and K fixed, because experts in an MoE share a shape - that is the constraint that makes grouped GEMM viable for MoE at all. Each expert segment must be aligned to the GEMM M block size, which is a hard layout requirement (get_mk_alignment_for_contiguous_layout). The masked variant exists because decode with CUDA graphs cannot know the token counts: the kernel takes a mask and computes only the valid portions, which trades a little wasted work inside tiles for removing a CPU sync from the critical path. Mega MoE is the different claim: it 'fuses and overlaps EP dispatch, linear 1 and linear 2 (FP8xFP4 or FP8xFP8), SwiGLU, and EP combine into a single mega-kernel, overlapping NVLink communication and tensor core computation' - that reduces both bytes (activations never round-trip HBM between the routed stages) and idle time (NVLink waits hidden behind MMA), at the cost of requiring a multi-process launch with a symmetric memory buffer.
scales_with: num_experts (group count, and the M-block alignment per expert)
experts_per_token
expert intermediate width
tokens per expert (the M dimension that determines whether the tile is efficient)
precision (fp8, fp4, bf16)
interconnect (Mega MoE's overlap is against NVLink)

flop_classes.name: DeepGEMM FP8/FP4 MQA scoring kernels for the lightning indexer
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The indexer computes, per token i and each KV token j in its span, a compressed scalar logit: reconstruct kv_j by applying the per-token KV scale (kv[0][j,:] * kv[1][j]), take q[i] . kv_j, apply ReLU, multiply by a per-head weight, and sum over heads. The FLOPs are a small GEMM per token against a reduced KV; what makes it a kernel is that KV is read in FP8/FP4 with MXFP4/MXFP8 data and packed UE8M0 scales on SM100, and the output is a dense [seq_len, max_seqlen_k] buffer whose row i holds only its valid KV span - i.e. it writes ragged scores into a rectangular tensor, which is a memory-layout and masking problem as much as a math problem. Two variants exist, non-paged for prefill and paged for decode, because the page indirection changes the KV access pattern.
scales_with: context_length
hidden_width
num_heads (the per-head weighted sum)
precision (fp8, fp4)

flop_classes.name: Per-token detokenisation, EOS/stop-string detection, and the host work they put on the critical path
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: This class has no bytes-per-flop at all: it is host-side text processing that runs once per generated token, on the API server's critical path, outside the model's arithmetic. Two costs, and they scale differently. (1) PER-TOKEN DETOKENISATION: the new token id is turned into text. In the shipped vLLM path this is a lookup into the tokenizer's DecodeStream plus the native incremental decode of that one piece - a vocab-table lookup (llama.cpp's token_to_piece consults a cache_token_to_piece table) and a UTF-8 decode of the piece.
