The published failure mode shows what the lookup can cost when it is written badly: detokenize_incrementally evaluated len(tokenizer) on EVERY generated token to range-check the id, and DeepseekV32Tokenizer.__len__ returned vocab_size + len(self.get_added_vocab()), where get_added_vocab() called into the native tokenizer each time - so a 1-token range check triggered a native added-vocab map rebuild/lookup (visible as BTreeMap::insert) on the GIL-holding main thread, once per token. (2) STOP-STRING DETECTION: per step, per stop string, a substring search over the newly generated characters. vLLM's check_stop_strings does output_text.find(stop_str, 1 - new_char_count - len(stop_str)) once PER STOP STRING, and it works because stop_buffer_length = max(len(s) for s in stop) - 1 characters are deliberately held back from the stream - so the scan window is bounded by new chars plus stop length, not by output length. That hold-back is the price of correctness at token boundaries: a stop string can straddle any token, so the engine must withhold up to max_stop_len - 1 characters and cannot emit them until it knows they are not part of a match. So the per-step cost is O(num_stop_strings x (new_chars + max_stop_len)) of host substring search plus O(bytes emitted) of holding, and it does NOT grow with sequence length - the one class in this family with a bounded per-step cost, provided the engine does the bounded-window search.
scales_with: num_generated_tokens (both costs run once per token, on the host, inside the streaming path)
num_stop_strings (one substring search per stop string per step)
max_stop_string_length (the hold-back is max(len(s)) - 1 characters, so a long stop string withholds a long tail of the stream and widens every scan window)
include_stop_str_in_output (when false, the hold-back applies and stop_buffer_length > 0; when true it is 0 and the scan window shrinks to the new characters)
vocab_size (only through the tokenizer's added-vocab / piece-cache lookup cost - a 152064-vocab tokenizer does more per-token lookup work than a 32000 one)
bytes emitted per token (a byte-level BPE token can decode to several characters, widening the stop-string scan window)
number of concurrent streams on one event loop (the per-token work is serialised on the GIL/loop, so it multiplies with concurrency rather than amortising)
byte-fallback / partial-UTF-8 handling (an incomplete trailing codepoint must be held, so some steps emit nothing at all)

flop_classes.name: Diffusion / masked-diffusion LMs: N denoising passes over the whole sequence instead of one token per forward pass
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: This inverts the decode cost model, so derive it explicitly. An AR model does 1 forward pass per generated token: flops = 2*N_active, and the per-token cost is flat because each pass sees only one new query position. A masked diffusion LM instead starts from a fully masked sequence of generation length Lg and runs S denoising steps, each a FULL forward pass over the current sequence: flops = S * 2*N_active * (attention over Lp+Lg instead of one row), where N_active is the whole model (diffusion LMs are dense). Take LLaDA 8B: config.json gives d_model 4096, mlp_hidden_size 12288, 8B params, max_sequence_length 4096. Per step flops = 2*N*(non-embedding) + attention = 2*8e9 for the weight GEMMs, plus attention over L tokens. The decisive point for serving: the number of tokens EMITTED per forward pass is Lg/S if each step unmasks one token (or the low-confidence-remask count per step, which LLaDA's semi-autoregressive block sampler controls). So effective flops per generated token = S*2*N/Lg, i.e. it scales with the step count S, not with a constant. LLaDA makes both knobs explicit: 'The total number of sampling steps is a hyperparameter, which naturally provides LLaDA with a trade-off between efficiency and sample quality' and 'the generation length is also treated as a hyperparameter, specifying the length of the fully masked sentence at the beginning of the sampling process.' Their sampling-efficiency ablation fixes generation length at 1024 for LLaDA 8B Base and tunes it from {64, 256, 512} for Instruct; Dream 7B (28 layers, hidden 3584, 4 KV heads per config.json) advertises 'tunable quality-speed trade-offs' and 'context-adaptive token-level noise rescheduling'. Arithmetic intensity is the second inversion: because every step is a full bidirectional forward pass, the query count equals the sequence length, so prefill-style arithmetic intensity applies to EVERY step and the per-token decode AI of ~1 flop/byte does not. Each step also re-reads the full weight set, so at S steps you pay S weight streams - unless the cache is reused, and LLaDA states the blocker plainly: 'We use vanilla multi-head attention instead of grouped query attention for simplicity, as LLaDA is incompatible with KV caching', and 'LLaDA does not use a causal mask, as its formulation allows it to see the entire input for predictions.' No cache means no incremental decode: every denoising step is a fresh full-attention pass over prompt+response.
scales_with: num_denoising_steps S (the master knob - flops per generated token scale linearly in it)
generation_length Lg (flops per step scale with the full sequence; tokens per step scale inversely with it, so flops/token ~ S/Lg)
num_layers and hidden_size (every step pays the full dense weight set - no expert sparsity to amortise)
prompt_length (full bidirectional attention over prompt+response every step, no causal exclusion)
remask strategy / block length (LLaDA's semi-autoregressive block length L' = 2/4/8/32/64 trades global coherence against wasted flops on not-yet-committed positions)

flop_classes.name: Diffusion LM practical serving: denoising steps, per-step cost, and throughput competitiveness vs AR decoding
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The serving picture for diffusion LMs is fundamentally different from AR. An AR model does 1 forward pass per token: flops = 2*N_active, constant per token. A diffusion LM does S denoising steps, each a full forward pass over the sequence: flops per step = 2*N_active + attention over L tokens. The total flops for generating Lg tokens is S * (2*N_active + attention). The effective flops per generated token is S * 2*N_active / Lg (if each step emits Lg/S tokens). For LLaDA 8B (d_model 4096, 8B params, max_seq 4096): per step flops = 2*8e9 = 16 GFLOP for the weight GEMMs alone, plus attention. With S=256 steps and Lg=1024 tokens: total flops = 256 * 16e9 = 4.1 TFLOP, effective flops per token = 4.1e12 / 1024 = 4 GFLOP/token. Compare AR: 2*8e9 = 16 GFLOP/token. So diffusion is 4x fewer flops per token in this configuration. But the wall-clock story is different: each step is a full forward pass with prefill-like arithmetic intensity, so it is compute-bound, not memory-bound. The weight stream is paid S times (unless cached), and there is no KV cache to reuse across steps (LLaDA: 'incompatible with KV caching'). The batch scaling is also different: diffusion's natural parallelism axis is the batch, not the sequence, so batch 1 is compute-bound while AR at batch 1 is memory-bound.
scales_with: num_denoising_steps S (the master knob — flops per token scale linearly in S)
generation_length Lg (flops per step scale with full sequence; tokens per step scale inversely)
num_layers and hidden_size (every step pays the full dense weight set)
prompt_length (full bidirectional attention over prompt+response every step)
remask strategy / block length

flop_classes.name: Dynamic resolution and any-resolution vision token cost
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Dynamic resolution approaches (NaViT, Pixtral, LLaVA-NeXT/AnyRes) allow the vision encoder to process images at their native resolution and aspect ratio, rather than resizing to a fixed grid. The token count is determined by the image dimensions: tokens = (H/patch_size) * (W/patch_size). For a 448x448 image with patch_size 14 and 2x2 spatial merge: (448/14/2)^2 = 16^2 = 256 tokens. For a 1024x1024 image with patch_size 16 and no merge: (1024/16)^2 = 64^2 = 4096 tokens. The token count is attacker-controlled via image size, which makes serving cost unpredictable.
scales_with: image_height (linear in tokens)
image_width (linear in tokens)
patch_size (inverse quadratic - smaller patches = more tokens)
spatial_merge_size (inverse quadratic - larger merge = fewer tokens)

flop_classes.name: Embedding lookup and output projection over the vocabulary
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Input embedding is a pure gather: ~0 flops against hidden_width*2 bytes read per token, so AI is effectively zero and it is strictly a memory-access pattern problem. The output side (LM head, untied) is a real GEMM: flops = 2*hidden_width*V against bytes = 2*hidden_width*V + 2*V, giving AI ~1 flop/byte at batch 1 - the same regime as decode_gemm, because it is literally a weight matrix of vocab_width. Tied embeddings mean one weight matrix serves both directions, but the lookup and the GEMM pull opposite access patterns: random row gather versus dense streaming. A batched input-embedding gather across B tokens has AI still ~0 - bytes scale with B exactly as flops do (there are no flops).
scales_with: vocab_size
hidden_width
batch_size (gather bytes scale linearly; AI unchanged)
tying (whether one matrix serves lookup and projection)

flop_classes.name: Embedding / batch encoding: BERT-style bi-encoder over documents, compute-bound at batch 1
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Batch encoding a corpus for retrieval is a bi-encoder forward per document with no KV cache, and like cross-encoder reranking it is compute-bound well before batch 1 - but unlike reranking its corpus cost is LINEAR, because each document is encoded once and its vector cached. The AI has two distinct regimes separated by an exactly computable batch threshold. With P parameters and t tokens per document: flops = B*2*P*t; bytes = 2*P (weights, read once for ALL B documents) + activation traffic. Ignoring activations, AI = B*t flop/byte. On H100 SXM with ridge 295.4 flop/byte (989.5 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s), the threshold is B*t = 295.4. Worked with BERT-base geometry (P = 113.2M, derived from d=768, 3072 intermediate, 12 layers, 12 heads x 64 head_dim) and the standard 128-token chunking used by sentence-embedding models: at B = 1, t = 128, AI = 128 flop/byte - just below the ridge, so a single-document encode is memory-bound; at B = 3, AI = 384 > 295.4 and it is compute-bound. At B = 8, AI = 1,024 (3.5x the ridge); at B = 64, AI = 8,192 (28x); at B = 256, AI = 32,768 (111x). Adding activation traffic lowers these: counting roughly 4 read/write passes over a B*t*d activation at bf16, at B = 1, t = 128 the activation term is ~4*128*768*2 = 786 KB against 226 MB of weights, so it is negligible - weights really do dominate - and the B*t figure stands. The practical statement: embedding a corpus is compute-bound for essentially every batch size a real encoder runs at, because a corpus is thousands of documents and the threshold B*t = 295 is crossed within the first few. Attention contributes almost nothing at these lengths: bidirectional attention flops = 2*2*n_q*dh*t^2 = 4*12*64*128^2 = 50.3 MFLOP against 2*113.2e6*128 = 29.0 GFLOP of GEMM = 0.17%. The crossover is L* = P_layer/(n_q*dh) = 9.44M/768 = 12,288 tokens, again far past realistic chunk sizes.
scales_with: batch_size B (AI = B*t - the threshold is B*t = 295.4 on H100, so B >= 3 at t = 128, and corpus work pushes B far above that)
chunk_length t (multiplies AI directly and linearly; long-document embedding without chunking raises AI and flops together)
corpus_size (flops scale LINEARLY, unlike reranking's quadratic - each document is encoded exactly once and the vector is cached)
model_size P (linear in flops; a 110M encoder is ~3x cheaper per document than a 300M one)
pooling_and_output_projection (a mean-pool or CLS head is negligible; a large projection head is a GEMM like any other)
precision (fp8/int8 encoder inference: at AI of thousands of flop/byte this converts directly to throughput)

flop_classes.name: Encoder-decoder vs decoder-only multimodal serving
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Encoder-decoder architectures (Whisper, Flamingo) process the input modality in a separate encoder, then decode the output autoregressively. The encoder runs once per input, the decoder runs once per output token. Decoder-only with visual tokens (LLaVA, Pixtral, Qwen2-VL) processes the entire input (text + visual tokens) in one prefill pass, then decodes autoregressively. The serving implication is that encoder-decoder architectures have a fixed encoder cost per input, while decoder-only architectures have a prefill cost that scales with total input length (text + visual).
scales_with: input_resolution (encoder-decoder: linear in encoder cost; decoder-only: linear in prefill cost)
output_length (both: linear in decode cost)
num_layers (both: linear)
model_width (both: quadratic in MLP, linear in attention)

flop_classes.name: The cost of one forward pass with no batching: the batch-1 decode-step formula, and the batch at which it stops being memory-bound
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: BATCH 1 IS A REGIME, NOT A SCALE. At batch 1 a decode step streams the whole weight set once and does one multiply-accumulate per weight, so AI = 2*P_flops/(w_b*P_bytes) = 2/w_b, where w_b is bytes per stored weight: exactly 1.0 flop/byte for bf16 (w_b=2), 2.0 for fp8/int8 (w_b=1), 4.0 for int4 (w_b=0.5). That is one to four flop/byte against ridge points of 150-810 flop/byte for every part in this repo, so batch-1 decode is memory-bound by a factor of 75-400x in bandwidth terms. THE FORMULA, with every input named: bytes_step = w_b*P_eff + 2*d*V*w_b (LM head, untied) + kv_b*tok * L (KV read) + kv_b*tok (KV write, one token) + activation/overhead bytes (see fct-overhead-flop-ledger). t_step = max(bytes_step/BW_eff, flops_step/PEAK_eff). flops_step = 2*P_eff + 2*d*V + attention and overhead terms. tok/s = 1/t_step. The batch-1 step is memory-bound iff bytes_step/BW > flops_step/PEAK, and since bytes_step and flops_step are both proportional to P_eff at batch 1, that inequality reduces to 1/AI < 1/AI_ridge, i.e. AI < AI_ridge, which is decided entirely by w_b and the machine. Worked: Llama-3-8B on one H100 SXM, bf16, L=1024, batch 1. P_eff (attention + MLP weights, excluding embeddings) = 32 layers x [(q: 4096x4096) + (k,v: 2 x 4096x1024) + (o: 4096x4096) + (mlp: 3 x 4096x14336)] = 32 x [16.78M + 8.39M + 16.78M + 176.16M] = 32 x 218.10M = 6.979e9. Weight bytes = 2 x 6.979e9 = 13.957e9 = 12.999 GiB. LM head untied = 2 x 4096 x 128256 = 1.051e9 = 0.979 GiB. KV read at L=1024 = 128 KiB/token x 1024 = 128 MiB = 0.125 GiB. Total 14.103 GiB = 1.514e10 bytes. t_mem = 1.514e10 / 3.350e12 = 4.520 ms. flops_step = 2 x 6.979e9 + 2 x 4096 x 128256 = 1.396e10 + 1.051e9 = 1.501e10; t_math = 1.501e10 / 989.5e12 = 15.2 us. Memory-bound by 298x. Predicted 221.2 tok/s at batch 1, L=1024, bf16, H100 SXM. THE CROSSOVER IS NOT A CONSTANT - it is B* = (PEAK/BW) x w_b/2, derived by setting AI(B) = AI_ridge where AI(B) = B/w_b for a weight GEMM (B tokens amortize each weight byte): H100 SXM (PEAK_bf16 989.5 TFLOPS, BW 3350 GB/s) gives AI_ridge = 295.4 flop/byte and therefore B* = 147.7 for bf16 (w_b=2), 295.4 for fp8 (w_b=1), 590.7 for int4 via dequant-to-bf16 (w_b=0.5), 73.8 for int4 with bf16 math only if the dequantized activation re-read dominates. Full table, all parts, all formats (each row is PEAK for the format actually EXECUTING divided by that part's own bandwidth, times w_b/2): H100 SXM 295.4 bf16 / 295.4 fp8 / 73.8 int4-dequant-to-bf16 / 147.7 int4-native; H200 SXM 206.1 / 206.1 / 51.5; MI300X 246.7 / 246.7 / 61.7; B200 312.5 / 312.5 / 312.5 (fp4 is native at 2x fp8, so w_b halves and PEAK doubles - the two cancel exactly, which is the cleanest possible demonstration that B* is a property of the memory system and not of the arithmetic); A100-80GB 153.0 / 153.0 / 38.3; RTX 4090 163.9 bf16 / 327.7 int4-native; L4 403.3 / 404.2; TPU v5e 240.5. The invariance is the finding: B* depends on PEAK/BW and w_b, so a part that gains bandwidth and FLOPS in the same proportion gains nothing, and quantization that raises PEAK in the same proportion as it cuts bytes gains nothing either. What moves B* is only a RATIO change between arithmetic and bandwidth. CONSEQUENCES THAT FALL OUT OF THE TABLE. (1) An L4 needs batch 403 to leave the memory wall on bf16, so a latency-serving L4 that never exceeds batch ~256 has never run a compute-bound decode step and every optimization aimed at tensor-core utilization was aimed at the wrong thing. (2) An RTX 4090 crosses at 164 (bf16), so the popular '4090 is a good local-inference part' claim is false for anything under batch ~164 but true above it, and the crossover is 2.5x sooner than an H100's - a bandwidth-rich FLOPS-poor part reaches the wall earlier and then has 6x less compute to do the work with. (3) Nothing crosses before batch ~50 on any part in this repo in a format that does not dequantize, so the entire low-batch serving regime is bandwidth-priced and every FLOP-side optimization is invisible there. The second crossover that matters at batch 1 is not arithmetic but bytes: KV bytes displace weight bytes in the step's byte budget as context grows, and the batch at which KV read equals the weight stream is B_kv = P_eff / (L * kv_b*tok) where kv_b*tok = 2*n_kv*head_dim*layers*kv_dtype_bytes. Numerically with Llama-2-70B geometry (P_eff = 68.98e9, kv_b*tok = 320 KiB): B_kv = 411 at L=1k, 51 at L=8k, 13 at L=32k, 3 at L=128k. Llama-3-8B (P_eff 8.03e9, 128 KiB/token): 120 at L=1k, 15 at L=8k, 3.7 at L=32k. Llama-2-7B with MHA (P_eff 6.74e9, 512 KiB/token): 25 at L=1k, 3.1 at L=8k, 0.8 at L=32k - i.e. at 32k context a single Llama-2-7B sequence reads MORE KV than it reads weights, and from batch 1 the step is KV-bound, which is a different bottleneck with a different fix (cache compression, sliding window, GQA) than the weight-stream wall.
scales_with: batch_size (the crossover knob: AI = B/w_b, so B* = (PEAK/BW)*w_b/2)
weight_bytes_per_param w_b (2 bf16, 1 fp8/int8, 0.5 int4 - scales B* linearly, and cancels against PEAK if PEAK scales with it too)
context_length (KV bytes displace weight bytes in the step's byte budget; the B_kv crossover above)
hidden_width and intermediate_size (both enter P_eff and, via the KV term, B_kv)
num_kv_heads and head_dim (set kv_b/token; MHA vs GQA-8 is a 4x or 8x swing in B_kv)
vocab_size (the LM head is a second full weight matrix when embeddings are untied)
tying (a tied LM head removes d*V bytes from every single step)

flop_classes.name: The energy form: deriving joules per token from watts and throughput, and from bytes and bandwidth when you have neither, with a stated error bound
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: TWO ROUTES, AND THE CHOICE BETWEEN THEM IS THE WHOLE SUBJECT. ROUTE 1 (measured watts) has ZERO model error and should always be preferred: E/token [J] = P_mean [W] / throughput [tok/s]. The only requirements are that P_mean is the MEAN over the same window that produced the token count, that the window excludes the ramp, that the clock state is recorded, and that the power scope is named (board / system / node / rack). This is the whole content of the MLPerf power methodology, and the repo's H200 records are the worked example: 5,806.9 W mean node draw against 25,262.1 output tok/s gives 0.2299 J/output token exactly, and 5,854.3 W against 48,987.9 tok/s gives 0.1195 J/token for Mixtral-8x7B on the same node, same instrument, same locked 1000 MHz clocks. ROUTE 2 (derived, for a number you have not measured) is a three-step chain and every step has an error term you must state. Step 1, step time: t_step = bytes_step / BW_eff in the memory-bound regime, with bytes_step = w_b*P_eff + 2*d*V*w_b + kv_b*tok*L + kv_b*tok + overhead bytes (the first two terms and the crossover condition are derived in fct-batch1-step-cost-formula). Worked: Llama-3-8B bf16 on H100 SXM at batch 1, L = 1024 - weights 12.999 GiB (13.957e9 bytes), LM head 0.979 GiB, KV read 0.125 GiB, total 14.103 GiB = 1.514e10 bytes, t_step = 1.514e10 / 3.350e12 = 4.520 ms, so 221.2 tok/s, against a compute time of 15.2 us for the same step (memory-bound by 298x). Step 2, power: P = eta * TDP_board, and eta is the term everyone gets wrong because it is not 1 and not constant. The repo has two anchors and they disagree in an instructive way: an 8xH200 node plateau of 5,806.9 W against a GPU nameplate of 8 x 700 = 5,600 W gives eta_loaded = 1.037 - ABOVE nameplate, legitimately, because the node also carries two Xeon 8480C hosts, 2 TB DRAM, ten 400 GbE NICs and PSU losses that are not in the GPU nameplate; and an 8xH100 node under compute-intensive TRAINING at 76% of its 10.2 kW rating gives eta = 0.76 - BELOW nameplate, with a calibrated model reaching 11.4% MAPE against 27-37% for TDP-based estimation. The lesson is not a number, it is a direction: TDP understates a loaded multi-GPU NODE (non-accelerator overhead is outside the GPU nameplate) and overstates a single accelerator or a lightly loaded one. Step 3, utilisation, and this is the term most cost models omit entirely: with P_idle = 2,411.2 W, P_loaded = 5,806.9 W and full-rate throughput R = 25,262.1 tok/s from the SAME H200 node, linear interpolation gives P(u) = P_idle + u*(P_loaded - P_idle) and tok/s(u) = u*R, so E/token(u) = [P_idle + u*(P_loaded - P_idle)] / (u*R) = P_loaded/R + (P_idle/R)*(1/u - 1). The first term is the floor at full utilisation and the second is the entire penalty for running below it: u = 1.00 -> 0.2299 J (1.00x); u = 0.75 -> 0.2617 J (1.14x); u = 0.50 -> 0.3253 J (1.42x); u = 0.25 -> 0.5162 J (2.25x); u = 0.15 -> 0.7707 J (3.35x); u = 0.10 -> 1.0889 J (4.74x); u = 0.05 -> 2.0434 J (8.89x). It DIVERGES as u -> 0, which is the correct behaviour and not a modelling artefact: the repo's idle record has 2,411.2 W at literally 0 tok/s, so the naive E = P/throughput division is a division by zero and the naive E = u*P_loaded approach at u = 0.15 gives 871 W where the honest figure is 2,921 W - 3.4x wrong in the direction that makes an underbatched fleet look cheap. THE STATED ERROR BOUND, decomposed so a reader can see which term dominates: for a Route-2 estimate of joules per token, the error sources are (i) utilisation modelling, P_idle/P_loaded linear in u, worth up to 4.7x at u = 0.10 and unbounded below - DOMINANT, and the only fix is to measure at the intended utilisation; (ii) TDP-vs-actual, empirically 27-37% MAPE for TDP-based power estimation against 11.4% for a calibrated architecture-specific model, so a TDP-based joules figure carries roughly that relative error; (iii) peak-vs-sustained throughput, where peak is a best case at maximum batch and a real deployment runs 20-50% lower, and this error is one-sided (it makes joules per token look too LOW, because TDP overstates power while peak throughput overstates tokens and the two do not cancel); (iv) model-size transfer, since energy per token scales with ACTIVE parameters, not total, so scaling a measured figure by total parameters is wrong for every MoE and the repo's own pair demonstrates it - Mixtral-8x7B at 0.1195 J/token draws essentially the same watts as the dense 70B at 0.2299 J (5,854.3 vs 5,806.9 W, under 1% apart) because only ~12.9B of its 46.7B parameters are active, so the per-token efficiency ratio of 1.92x comes entirely from active-parameter sparsity; (v) power scope, where board-level to system-level is a 1.4-1.7x factor on datacenter nodes and a 20-50x factor on Apple silicon (4.4 mJ/token package against 0.09 J/token system for the same 3B model). ADDING (i)-(iv) IN QUADRATURE gives 30-50% for a TDP-based estimate at moderate utilisation, which matches the error bound already recorded in this repo, and the bound is only honest if the reader is told WHICH term dominates: at u < 0.25 the utilisation term alone exceeds the whole stated error bar. The cleanest single sanity check available to a reader with no meter: compare the model's implied bytes-per-joule against hardware bandwidth. 221.2 tok/s at, say, 700 W board gives 3.16 J/s per 221.2 tokens = 14.3 mJ/token, and 14.1 GiB per step at 3.35 TB/s means a memory-bound step CANNOT exceed about 238 tok/s on one H100 - so any joules-per-token figure implying more than 238 tokens/s from one H100 is arithmetically impossible and can be rejected without a power meter at all.
scales_with: utilisation (the dominant term: E/token diverges as 1/u below the full-rate power point)
active_parameters_per_token (not total parameters - the MoE case moves energy per token 1.9x at identical watts)
batch_size (via bytes_step, hence t_step, hence tokens per joule at fixed watts)
context_length (via the KV term in bytes_step)
weight_dtype (w_b halves the step's bytes and therefore halves the step's time at batch 1, so the same watts buy 2x the tokens)
power_scope (board vs system vs node vs rack, worth 1.4-1.7x on datacenter nodes and 20-50x on integrated packages)
clock_state (a locked 1000 MHz run is not a stock-boost run; the efficiency direction of the difference is unknown without both)
model_size (linear for active parameters in the memory-bound regime; the Apple silicon measurement shows 2.6x spread across 3-9B models holding hardware, engine and precision constant)

flop_classes.name: The overhead FLOP ledger: norms, RoPE, activations, softmax, residuals, KV-cache writes and sampling priced per decode step, fused versus unfused
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: THE HEADLINE IS A BYTE RESULT, NOT A FLOP RESULT, AND THAT IS THE POINT. The elementwise classes carry real flops but almost no arithmetic intensity, so they are invisible in a FLOP count and dominant in a bandwidth count. Per decode step, per token-slot, per layer, with d = hidden, I = intermediate, n_q = query heads, n_kv = KV heads, d_h = head_dim, and n_layers: RMSNorm x2 (input_layernorm and post_attention_layernorm): flops = 2 x 4d = 8d (d multiplies to form x^2, d adds, d multiplies by the gain weight, d multiplies by the normalized reciprocal-RMS), bytes = 2 x 3d x s (read x, read gain, write y), so AI = 8d/6d = 1.33 flop/byte at s = 2; residual add x2: flops = 2d, bytes = 2 x 3d x s (read two tensors, write one), AI = 0.33; RoPE on Q and K: elements = 2(n_q + n_kv)*d_h, flops ~ 1.5 per element for the rotate-half form (two multiplies and one add per rotated pair, and half the tensor is rotated), bytes = 2 x elements x s (read and write), AI = 0.19 - the WORST intensity of any class here, because RoPE is applied to a tensor two orders of magnitude smaller than the FFN and is almost always a separate kernel; SwiGLU activation: flops = 4dI for silu (exp, add, div, mul) plus dI for the gate multiply = 5dI against the FFN's own 6dI, i.e. the activation is 83% of the FFN's flops while being 0% of its bytes when fused into the GEMM epilogue; UNFUSED it costs 3 x dI x s bytes (read gate, read up, write the product) which at AI 0.83 is the single largest byte consumer in the entire decode step; softmax over scores: flops = 5 x L x n_q (max, subtract, exp, sum, divide), bytes UNFUSED = 2 x L x n_q x s (write the scores, read them back) = the L x n_q score matrix materialized twice, AI 0.625; with an online-softmax attention kernel those bytes are ZERO because the scores never leave SRAM/registers - this is the single biggest byte saving in the whole ledger and is what FlashAttention bought; KV cache write: flops = 0 exactly, bytes = 2 x n_kv x d_h x kv_bytes per layer per token - a pure store, 4,096 bytes per layer per token for GQA-8 at head_dim 128 and bf16, giving 128 KiB/token for Llama-3-8B, 320 KiB/token for Llama-2-70B, 256 KiB/token for Qwen3-32B, and 512 KiB/token for MHA Llama-2-7B; sampler (softmax + top-k + renormalize + draw): flops ~ 5V, bytes = 2 x 2 x V (fp32 logits read and write) at the fp32 cast vLLM performs unconditionally, AI ~1.25. LEDGER, ALL FOUR CLASSES, BATCH 1, L = 1024, bf16, with the step's weight stream for comparison (Llama-3-8B: 14.0 GF of GEMM flops against 15,009 MB of weight bytes; Llama-2-70B: 136.9 GF against 137,426 MB; Qwen3-32B: 60.4 GF against 61,954 MB): Llama-3-8B (d=4096, I=14336, 32/8 heads, d_h=128, 32 layers, V=128256) - RMSNorm x2 0.0010 GF / 1.573 MB / AI 0.67 (using the s=2 byte count: 2 x 3 x 4096 x 2 x 32 = 1.573 MB); residual x2 0.0003 GF / 1.573 MB / AI 0.17; RoPE 0.0005 GF / 2.621 MB / AI 0.19; SwiGLU 9.395 GF / 11,274 MB / AI 0.83; softmax 0.0052 GF / 8.389 MB / AI 0.63; KV write 0 GF / 0.131 MB; sampler 0.0006 GF / 0.513 MB / AI 1.25. UNFUSED TOTAL 9.40 GF against 11,289 MB = 75.2% of the step's HBM bytes, AI 0.83. FUSED TOTAL (SwiGLU into the GEMM epilogue, softmax inside the attention kernel) 9.40 GF against 6.28 MB = 0.04% of the step's bytes. Llama-2-70B (d=8192, I=28672, 64/8 heads, 80 layers, V=32000): UNFUSED 93.99 GF / 112,812 MB = 82.1% of the step's bytes; FUSED 27.66 MB = 0.02%. Qwen3-32B (d=5120, I=25600, 64/8 heads, 64 layers, V=151936): UNFUSED 41.97 GF / 50,383 MB = 81.3%; FUSED 17.91 MB = 0.03%. THE RESULT THAT MATTERS: left unfused, the elementwise classes are 75-82% of all the HBM bytes a batch-1 decode step moves - MORE than the weights. Fused, they are under 0.05%. This is not a marginal optimization; it is the difference between a decode step that reads 14 GiB and one that reads 26 GiB. The FLOP side is the mirror image and must not be conflated: the overhead classes carry 67-69% as many flops as the step's GEMMs (9.40 GF against 14.0 GF for Llama-3-8B, 94.0 against 136.9 for the 70B, 42.0 against 60.4 for Qwen3-32B), almost all of it in SiLU's exp and the softmax's exp. Those flops execute on the ALU and SFU, not on the tensor cores, at roughly 1/30th the bf16 tensor-core rate on H100, so 69% more flops that run 30x slower contribute about 2% of the step's time when memory-bound - and become the dominant term when the step is compute-bound, which is the regime where a fused, SFU-friendly activation kernel is worth having. Batch invariance: every one of these terms is linear in B, so the overhead's SHARE of the step is invariant to batch (Llama-3-8B at B = 64: UNFUSED 601.8 GF / 722,461 MB = 75.2%, identical to B = 1). That invariance is the useful structural fact: fusion decisions taken at batch 1 remain correct at batch 256, but the overhead's share of BYTES only falls if the FLOP side of the ledger grows faster than its byte side, which happens only when you move from elementwise kernels into a compute-bound regime.
scales_with: fused_vs_unfused (the dominant lever by a factor of 1800 on bytes: 11,289 MB unfused vs 6.28 MB fused on Llama-3-8B)
intermediate_size (SwiGLU's byte cost is 3*d*I*s per layer, the largest single overhead byte term when unfused)
hidden_width (every norm, residual and rope term is linear in d)
num_attention_heads x head_dim (RoPE and softmax terms)
vocab_size (the sampler, and the fp32 cast that doubles it)
context_length (softmax's L x n_q materialization; ZERO under FlashAttention)
kv_dtype_bytes (the KV write, which is the only overhead term with zero flops)
batch_size (all terms linear - the overhead share is batch-invariant)

flop_classes.name: Prefill FLOP crossover: the context length at which attention equals the MLP, computed per architecture family from each model's own config
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: THE CROSSOVER IS A CONFIG RATIO, NOT A CONTEXT NUMBER. Within one prefill of L tokens, per layer: attention flops = 2*n_q*head_dim*L^2 (causal: the two L x L score/output matmuls each contribute 2*n_q*head_dim*L^2 before halving, and the mask halves both, so the factor 2 already includes it); GEMM flops = 2*P_layer*L. Setting them equal gives L* = P_layer / (n_q*head_dim) - a pure parameter ratio with NO hardware in it and no context in it. And the true share of prefill flops is not L/L* but A(L) = L/(L + L*), because the two terms add rather than compete; A(L*) = 50% by construction. Where n_q*head_dim = hidden_size (the normal case), L* = P_layer/hidden_size, which is roughly the feed-forward expansion ratio plus the attention projections - so L* is a number in the tens of thousands for a dense transformer and the crossover is NEVER reached inside a normal context window. THE TABLE, every geometry read from the model's own config.json (head counts, head_dim, intermediate_size), P_layer computed as q: d*n_q*d_h, k and v: 2*d*n_kv*d_h, o: n_q*d_h*d, mlp: 3*d*I (gate, up, down): Llama-2-7B (MHA, d=4096, I=11008, n_q=32, n_kv=32, d_h=128) P_layer = 202,375,168, n_q*d_h = 4096, L* = 49,408; Llama-2-13B (MHA, d=5120, I=13824, 40 heads, 40 KV heads) P_layer = 317,194,240, n_q*d_h = 5120, L* = 61,952; Llama-2-70B (GQA-8, d=8192, I=28672, n_q=64, n_kv=8) P_layer = 855,638,016, n_q*d_h = 8192, L* = 104,448; Llama-3-8B (GQA-4, d=4096, I=14336, 32/8 heads) P_layer = 218,103,808, L* = 53,248; Mistral-7B-v0.1 (GQA-4, d=4096, I=14336, 32/8) P_layer = 218,103,808, L* = 53,248 - IDENTICAL to Llama-3-8B because the two configs are geometrically identical, which is a real property of those two models and not a transcription error; Mixtral-8x7B (top-2 of 8, d=4096, I_expert=14336, 32/8) P_layer = 394,264,576, L* = 96,256 - 1.8x Llama-3-8B because the dense Llama layer activates 3*4096*14336 of MLP weight while Mixtral's top-2 activates 3*4096*14336 too but the expert count changes routing, not active width, so the increase is from counting the expert FFN at full per-expert width while the Llama number counts one FFN; Qwen3-32B (dense, d=5120, I=25600, n_q=64, n_kv=8, d_h=128) P_layer = 487,587,840, n_q*d_h = 8192, L* = 59,520; Qwen3-30B-A3B (top-8 of 128, d=2048, I_expert=768, moe_intermediate=768, 32/4 heads, d_h=128) P_layer = 56,623,104, n_q*d_h = 4096, L* = 13,824 - and THIS is the row that matters, because it is 4x lower than any dense model in the table. ATTENTION SHARE A(L) = L/(L+L*) at 1k / 8k / 32k / 128k: Llama-2-7B 2.0% / 14.2% / 39.9% / 72.6%; Llama-2-13B 1.6% / 11.7% / 34.6% / 67.9%; Llama-2-70B 1.0% / 7.3% / 23.9% / 55.7%; Llama-3-8B 1.9% / 13.3% / 38.1% / 71.1%; Mistral-7B 1.9% / 13.3% / 38.1% / 71.1%; Mixtral-8x7B 1.1% / 7.8% / 25.4% / 57.7%; Qwen3-32B 1.7% / 12.1% / 35.5% / 68.8%; Qwen3-30B-A3B 6.9% / 37.2% / 70.3% / 90.5%. TWO FAMILIES BREAK THE FORM, and both are why a single number is wrong. (1) HYBRID attention-SSM: only the attention layers have an L^2 term, so divide L* by the attention-layer fraction. Nemotron-H-8B (52 layers, hybrid_override_pattern gives exactly 4 attention layers, d=4096, I=21504, 32/8 heads, d_h=128): dense-layer P_layer = 306,184,192 so L* = 74,752 for a full-attention layer, but 4/52 = 0.0769 of layers are attention, so the effective crossover is L*_eff = 5,750 and A(L) = 15.1% at 1k, 58.8% at 8k, 85.1% at 32k - a hybrid model is an attention-dominated model at 8k where a dense Llama of the same size is at 13%. Gemma-3-27B (62 layers, sliding_window 1024 with sliding_window_pattern 6, so 1 layer in 6 attends globally and 5 attend only to the last 1024 tokens, d=5376, I=21504, 32/16 heads, d_h=128): P_layer = 412,876,800, L* = 100,800 for a global layer, and since only the 1-in-6 global layers have an L^2 term the effective crossover is 16,800, giving 5.7% / 32.8% / 66.1%. The correct treatment for Gemma-3 is not a single L* at all: attention flops are A_global(1/6)*L^2/2 + A_local(5/6)*min(L,1024)^2/2, so beyond L = 1024 the local layers stop growing and only the global layer's L^2 term remains - which is why a sliding-window model has an attention share that PLATEAUS instead of rising toward 1. (2) MLA (latent attention): DeepSeek-V3 compresses K and V into a 512-rank latent, so per-layer attention flops = 2*n_q*(kv_lora_rank + qk_rope_head_dim)*L^2 for QK plus 2*n_q*v_head_dim*L^2 for PV, i.e. the denominator n_q*head_dim is replaced by n_q*(192 + 128) = 40,960 in the QK half and n_q*128 = 16,384 in the PV half - an effective ~28,672 against P_layer = 866,123,776 (top-8 of 256 routed experts at moe_intermediate 2048 plus one shared expert), giving L* ~ 52,864 on the PV half alone and ~30,205 on the QK half, so MLA's crossover is in the same range as a dense model's while its KV BYTES are 85x smaller. Two consequences a reader should carry away. FIRST, the crossover is not a hardware property at all: it is P_layer/(n_q*head_dim), computed from a config file, identical on every part. Hardware decides only WHICH side of the crossover a given prefill falls on, via the ridge crossings L_ridge = 2*AI_ridge/g from prefill-attention (591 tokens for MHA on H100, 148 for GQA-4) - which are hundreds of tokens, not tens of thousands. So in every configuration in this table, prefill is already compute-bound long before the attention share is significant, and the two numbers answer different questions. SECOND, the direction of the comparison surprises people: a WIDER model defers the crossover (Llama-2-70B at 104,448 vs Llama-2-13B at 61,952) while a MOE model with a narrow hidden size advances it enormously (Qwen3-30B-A3B at 13,824), because L* is a ratio of per-token GEMM width to attention width and MoE deliberately shrinks the numerator. A 30B MoE is therefore far more attention-bound than a 32B dense model, which is a fact about the config and not about the parameter count.
scales_with: context_length (attention share = L/(L+L*), rising monotonically toward 1 for dense attention)
intermediate_size I (numerator of L* via 3*d*I - the single biggest lever)
num_attention_heads x head_dim (denominator of L* - note these need not equal hidden_size; Qwen3 sets head_dim independently)
attention-layer fraction (the divisor for hybrid attention-SSM models: Nemotron-H 4/52, Gemma-3 1/6 global)
sliding_window (caps the local layers' L^2 term, which makes the attention share plateau instead of rising)
active_experts_per_token (numerator of L* for MoE - top-8 of 128 gives a far smaller numerator than a dense FFN of the same model size)
kv_lora_rank (denominator for MLA's QK half)

flop_classes.name: Speculative decoding cost model: the break-even acceptance rate a(B, k, draft size) actually requires, and the draft model's HBM cost against KV cache
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: THE COST MODEL, with each term defined. Baseline decode step at batch B: T_base(B) = max(2*P_t/BW, 2*B*P_t/PEAK) for the target's weight stream alone, with P_t the target parameter count and the same terms added for KV. One speculative iteration that drafts k positions and expects a accepted tokens (a = expected accepted tokens per pass, INCLUDING the bonus token, so 1 <= a <= k+1) costs: T_draft = max(2*P_d/BW, 2*k*P_d/PEAK) (draft weights streamed once, k positions of work) + T_verify = max(2*P_t/BW, 2*B*k*P_t/PEAK) (target weights streamed once, B*k rows of work). Serial execution sums them; if the two weight streams can be co-scheduled on the same memory system the tighter bound is T_spec = max(2*(P_d+P_t)/BW, 2*k*P_d/PEAK + 2*B*k*P_t/PEAK), and the honest answer is the serial sum minus whatever overlap the engine actually achieves - which is a measurement, not a derivation, so both bounds are given. SPEEDUP S = a / (T_spec / T_base) = a*T_base/T_spec, so BREAK-EVEN IS A_be = T_spec / (k * T_base). This is the number the repo was missing: a quoted speculative speedup is meaningless without the a_be it has to beat, and a_be is a function of batch, k, draft size AND the hardware's PEAK/BW ratio. WHY B DOES NOT APPEAR AT LOW BATCH, which is the non-obvious part: in the memory-bound regime both T_base and T_verify are dominated by the weight stream, and the target's weight stream is IDENTICAL in a baseline step and a verify pass - the verify pass reads the same 2*P_t bytes whether it computes 1 position or k, because k positions share every weight. So T_verify = T_base exactly while both are bandwidth-priced, and A_be collapses to (2*P_d/BW + 2*P_t/BW) / (k * 2*P_t/BW) = (1 + P_d/P_t)/k. BATCH IS ABSENT FROM THAT EXPRESSION. The whole 'speculation's advantage decays with batch' effect is therefore NOT a memory-bandwidth effect at low batch - it is the transition out of the memory-bound regime. WORKED, target P_t = 68.98e9 (Llama-2-70B), draft P_d = 1e9, k = 4, H100 SXM (BW 3350 GB/s, PEAK_bf16 989.5 TFLOPS): memory-bound regime A_be = (1 + 1/68.98)/4 = 1.0145/4 = 0.2536. BATCH SWEEP at k=4, P_d = 1e9, showing where B finally appears: B=1 to 64 all give A_be = 0.2536 identically (T_base = 2*P_t/BW = 41.18 ms; T_verify = the same 41.18 ms; T_draft = 0.597 ms; T_spec = 41.78 ms); B=128 T_verify is still bandwidth-priced but the compute term has started to matter - A_be = 0.4370 serial, 0.4334 overlapped; B=192 A_be = 0.654; B=256 A_be = 0.870; B=320 A_be = 1.003 and at this point T_base has ALSO crossed into compute pricing, so the regime has changed and the shape of the model changes with it; above B = B* (295.4 for bf16 on H100) both baseline and verify are compute-priced and A_be = (P_d + B*P_t)/(B*P_t) = 1 + P_d/(B*P_t), which tends to 1 as B grows. THE HEADLINE CONSEQUENCE: the memory-bound A_be of 0.2536 is trivially beatable - you need to accept only one token per four drafted positions, i.e. a 25% acceptance rate, and the maximum possible is k+1 = 5, so the available speedup range is up to 5/0.2536 = 19.7x and almost any real drafter lands in the middle of it. The compute-bound A_be of ~1.0 is much harder: you need essentially every drafted token accepted, and since a <= k+1 with equality only if the draft equals the target, the achievable window shrinks to almost nothing. This is the quantitative form of 'speculative decoding is a latency optimization, not a throughput one'. K AND DRAFT SIZE SWEEPS (memory-bound, hence B-independent, H100, P_t = 68.98e9): A_be = (1+P_d/P_t)/k, so at k=2, 0.5072; k=4, 0.2536; k=6, 0.1691; k=8, 0.1268; k=12, 0.0845 - linear in 1/k, so the required acceptance rate falls as 1/k but the MAXIMUM is k+1, so larger k widens the window on both sides and is nearly free in the memory-bound regime. Draft size at k=4: P_d = 0.4e9 gives 0.2514, 1e9 gives 0.2536, 7e9 gives 0.2754, 13e9 gives 0.2971 - the draft size enters only through P_d/P_t and is therefore almost irrelevant in the memory-bound regime (a 32x larger draft costs 17% more break-even acceptance) and dominant in the compute-bound one (A_be = 1 + P_d/(B*P_t), where P_d = 13e9 at B = 256 is 1 + 0.0005, still small, but at B = 8 it is 1.024). THE DRAFT'S MEMORY COST, which competes with KV cache directly: the draft weights are a FIXED byte cost 2*P_d that is amortized over B*L*kv_b*tok bytes of KV, so the draft is a large fraction of HBM exactly when KV is small, i.e. at low batch and short context. Numerically, a 1e9-parameter draft in bf16 is 1.863 GiB and is worth exactly 1.863 GiB / kv_b*tok tokens of KV: Llama-2-70B (320 KiB/token) 6,104 tokens; Llama-3-32B (256 KiB/token) 7,629; Llama-3-8B (128 KiB/token) 15,259. So at L = 4096 the draft's bytes are 67% (70B), 54% (32B), 27% (8B) of the whole KV cache. But at batch 32 and L = 32k the ordering inverts completely: Llama-2-70B KV = 320 GiB against a 1.87 GiB draft = 0.58% of the KV and 0.42% of the combined weights + KV footprint; Llama-3-8B KV = 128 GiB, draft = 1.46% of KV and 1.29% of the footprint. THE TWO FACTS RECONCILE: 'the draft competes with KV cache' is true only at low batch and short context; at production batch and context it is a rounding error, and the real cost of the draft is its LATENCY (it sits in the critical path of every iteration) and its weight bytes, not its share of HBM.
scales_with: acceptance_rate (the a in S = a*T_base/T_spec; break-even is A_be = T_spec/(k*T_base))
draft_k (A_be falls as 1/k in the memory-bound regime, so k is nearly free there)
draft_model_size P_d (enters as P_d/P_t; near-irrelevant memory-bound, dominant compute-bound)
batch_size (ABSENT from the memory-bound A_be and decisive in the compute-bound one: A_be = 1 + P_d/(B*P_t))
context_length (via KV bytes in both T_base and T_verify)
peak_to_bandwidth_ratio (B* = (PEAK/BW)*w_b/2 sets where B appears in the model at all)
overlap_achieved (serial sum vs bandwidth-shared bound; a measurement, not a derivation)

flop_classes.name: FlashAttention-2 work partitioning: fixing warp-level underutilization
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: No change to bytes or FLOPs relative to FA-1. FA-2 is a pure scheduling fix: it removes idle tensor-core cycles caused by poor thread-block/warp partitioning and redundant shared-memory traffic, i.e. it converts achieved FLOPs/s toward the FLOPs the tiles already imply. The metric that moves is MMA utilization (percent of tensor-core peak), not arithmetic intensity. Recorded as custom_kernel because the mechanism is kernel-organization, not an operation class.
scales_with: num_SMs (partitioning determines whether all SMs get equal work)
seqlen (partition granularity relative to seqlen)
batch_size

flop_classes.name: FlashAttention-3 (Hopper): warp specialization, TMA, and FP8 to overlap matmul with softmax
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Three different reductions, worth keeping separate. (1) Bytes: TMA (cp.async.bulk.tensor) does address generation and out-of-bounds predication in hardware, freeing registers, which lets the tile be larger - larger tiles amortize each HBM->SMEM byte over more FLOPs. (2) Occupancy of non-tensor units: the binding change is that softmax exponentials run on the SFU/MUFU path in the shadow of tensor-core work via warp specialization (producer warps issue TMA, consumer warps issue WGMMA) and ping-pong / 2-stage interleaving. On H100 SXM5 the tensor cores do 989 TFLOPS FP16 but only 3.9 TFLOPS of special functions (16 ops/SM/clock * 132 SM * 1.83 GHz), and at head_dim 128 there are ~512x more matmul than exponential FLOPs - so without overlap, exp can take 50% of the time of the matmuls, and in FP8 it gets worse because matmul doubles while exp does not. (3) FLOPs/precision: FP8 doubles tensor-core throughput (1978 vs 989 TFLOPS on H100), and incoherent processing (Hadamard transform with random signs, O(d log d), fusable into the RoPE pass) cuts FP8 quantization error 2.6x in the author's synthetic-outlier test.
scales_with: head_dim (exp cost per matmul flop scales inversely with head_dim)
precision (fp8 doubles tensor-core flops but leaves SFU exp unchanged)
seqlen
num_SMs (warp specialization needs enough warps per CTA to split roles)

flop_classes.name: FlashAttention-4 (Blackwell): tensor memory, 2-CTA MMA, and emulated exponential
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: FA-4 is the first attention kernel whose bottleneck moves off tensor cores. Feed-and-speeds per B200 SM at M=N=D=128: tensor cores 8192 ops/cycle, exponential unit 16 ops/cycle, shared memory 128 bytes/cycle. Forward per tile: 1024 tensor-core cycles vs 1024 exp cycles vs 768 SMEM cycles - forward is bound by compute AND exponential simultaneously. Backward (5 chained MMAs): 2560 tensor-core, 1024 exp, 3328 SMEM - backward is bound by SHARED-MEMORY BANDWIDTH, not FLOPs. So the reductions are: (1) shared-memory traffic in backward, via storing transposed intermediates directly into tensor memory in the operand-A layout the dV/dK MMAs consume (removing a shared-memory round trip) and via 2-CTA MMA which roughly halves operand-B shared-memory traffic; (2) SFU exp contention in forward, by splitting exp across hardware MUFU.EX2 and a software Cody-Waite + Horner polynomial on FMA units that would otherwise idle, and by explicitly desynchronizing the two softmax warpgroups so they do not contend for MUFU; (3) non-critical-path work, by moving online-softmax rescaling to a dedicated correction warpgroup and only rescaling when the max jump exceeds a threshold tau (the final output is still normalized by the true final statistics, so output is preserved); (4) register pressure, because UMMA accumulators live in TMEM rather than registers - Hopper-era FA-3's register pressure forced a more serial schedule.
scales_with: head_dim
tile size (FA-4 uses two 128-token query tiles per CTA)
seqlen
batch_size (scheduling: LPT ordering and batch-head swizzling into L2-sized sections to fight causal load imbalance)

flop_classes.name: FlashAttention IO-aware tiling (FA1): eliminating the S x S HBM round trip
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Does not raise AI arithmetically - the FLOP count of causal attention is unchanged. It removes bytes: the naive path writes the L x L score matrix to HBM and reads it back, adding Theta(L^2) HBM traffic on top of the Theta(L*d) KV traffic, which drops the effective AI from Theta(L) to well below the ridge point for most lengths. FA-1's tiling loads Q/K/V blocks HBM->SRAM once, keeps the running softmax accumulator in registers and never writes S to HBM, so bytes revert to the Theta(L*d) ideal. The claim to make precisely is 'reduces HBM traffic by removing the S x S materialization', NOT 'reduces attention FLOPs'.
scales_with: context_length (the bytes saved scale as L^2, the useful KV bytes as L)
batch_size (all batch sequences become one big GEMM pair)
head_dim (the S tile size per KV byte loaded)

flop_classes.name: FlashDecoding / split-KV attention: turning a single-token decode into a bandwidth-saturating GEMM
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The problem it solves is parallelism, not arithmetic. At batch 1 the decode step's attention has L query rows total, so a non-split kernel launches far fewer CTAs than the GPU has SMs and runs at a small fraction of memory bandwidth while the KV cache streams from HBM. Split-KV divides the KV sequence across S thread blocks, each computing a partial softmax, then merges the S partials with log-sum-exp in a second kernel. Bytes read from HBM are identical (every KV element still read once) and FLOPs are identical plus a small merge cost; what changes is achieved bandwidth and SM utilization. Recorded as decode_attention because that is the class it serves; the same mechanism appears inside FA-2 2.2 ('we split the loading across different thread blocks, with a separate kernel to combine results' for iterative decoding with very small query seqlen).
scales_with: context_length (the more KV there is to split, the more the split pays)
batch_size (as batch rises the split count needed falls, and eventually the split is unnecessary)
num_kv_heads and head_dim
num_SMs (the split count is capped by SM availability and by the combine kernel's cost)

flop_classes.name: FlashInfer: a kernel-selection layer over FlashAttention, cuDNN, CUTLASS and TensorRT-LLM
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: FlashInfer is not itself an arithmetic mechanism; it is the layer where backend choice decides which arithmetic is done. Recorded as custom_kernel because the engine-level effect is a discrete change in the kernels executing the same math. Its kernels change the bytes/FLOPs trade by adding: paged and ragged KV-cache layouts (so decode reads a gathered block table instead of a dense cache - same FLOPs, different access pattern and potentially more uncoalesced reads), cascade attention (a hierarchical pass that reads a shared prefix KV once and reuses it across requests rather than per-request, which cuts HBM bytes for shared prefixes), POD-attention (fused prefill+decode for a mixed batch, saving a kernel boundary and the re-read of the shared prefix), block-sparse and variable block-sparse plans, and FP8/FP4 GEMM and MoE paths (per-tensor, groupwise, NVFP4 and MXFP4 block-scaled) which do change the FLOP cost by doubling or quadrupling tensor-core throughput.
scales_with: batch_size (decode vs prefill vs mixed-batch kernel selection)
context_length
prefix sharing rate (cascade attention's benefit)
num_kv_heads and head_dim

flop_classes.name: FlashMLA decode: FP8/FP4 KV cache with scales inlined per token (DeepSeek MLA)
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The mechanism is a change in bytes moved, achieved by changing the KV cache element size, not by changing the attention math. MLA decode reads one KV head per token instead of a full K and V pair per head, so the cache is already much smaller than a GQA cache; FlashMLA pushes that to quantized cache formats. V4.1 (head_dim 512) stores 528 bytes/token: 512 bytes of float8_e4m3 over all 512 dims plus 16 bytes of float8_e8m0 scales, one scale per 32 consecutive e4m3 values. The fp4 variant is 288 bytes/token: 256 bytes of e2m1 (two values per byte, even index in the low nibble) plus 32 bytes of float8_e4m3 scales, one per 16 e2m1 values, valid only for extra_k_cache when k_cache is in the V4.1 format. The scales are stored in the same contiguous token record as the data, which is what lets the kernel dequantize in-register without a second scale fetch. FLOPs are unchanged except that the PV product and the dequant run in lower precision; the win is that KV bytes per token drop from bf16 (1024 bytes for the 512-dim head, K-side) to 528 or 288, i.e. roughly 2x or 3.5x less KV traffic for the same context.
scales_with: context_length (the whole point - traffic scales with it)
head_dim
num_kv_heads
kv cache precision (fp8 vs fp4 vs bf16)
token-level sparsity (the indices tensor makes decode compute only the selected top-k tokens)

flop_classes.name: FlashMLA fused norm-RoPE-attention-RoPE-cast kernel: absorbing per-token scalar work into the attention kernel
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: This kernel changes nothing about the attention arithmetic; it removes kernels and bytes at the boundaries. It fuses Q-norm (V4 only, not V4.1), Q-RoPE, core attention, the conjugate O-RoPE and the cast of the output to FP8 into a single kernel. Each of those steps on its own is memory-bound elementwise work over the same tensors, so fusing them removes one HBM round trip per step and one kernel launch each. The stated cost is that Q_b and the Wv weights must be permuted in advance - i.e. the mechanism is paid for with an offline layout change, which is a real constraint because it makes the weight preparation model-specific. Author claim: the fused kernel still reaches the same or slightly higher TFlops while eliminating the small-kernel overhead, and the decode path of the fused kernel was optimized 10-15% in the 2026.09.30 release.
scales_with: hidden_width (elementwise norm/RoPE/cast cost is proportional to width, not to context)
context_length (only through the attention part)
batch_size (fewer launches matters most at small batch)

flop_classes.name: Host-side sampling loop: full-logits D2H transfer plus the CPU sampler chain
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: This is the same V-wide tensor the sampling record describes, but measured in HOST time rather than device bytes, and that changes the answer by four orders of magnitude. On the device the logit read is negligible - 4*128256 = 501.0 KiB per token at fp32 against a Llama-3-8B batch-1 decode step that streams 2*8.03e9 = 16.06 GB of weights, i.e. 0.0031% of the step's bytes, and ~0.15 us of H100 time at 3350 GB/s. If a sampler reads those logits from HBM on the device and never ships them anywhere, it is free. But llama.cpp's default server path moves the ENTIRE logits row to the host every decode step: at one slot the issue measures 608.3 KB per D2H copy and identifies it as exactly 152064 vocab x 4 B = 608,256 B, one complete fp32 logits row, occurring once per step (938 copies in a 10 s window at ~94 decode steps/s); at 32 slots the same per-step copy measures 16,157.4 KB, which is at most 32 rows (32 x 608,256 B = 19,464,192 B) and in practice fewer because slots are not all resident every step. Then the CPU walks it. CPU sampling of on-CPU samples landing inside >=1 ms GPU idle gaps at 32 slots attributes 45.2% to common_sampler_sample() and 12.7% to llama_token_data_array_partial_sort_inplace(), 58.6% of in-gap host time to the sampler in total. The C++ source explains why top_k does not save you: llama_token_data_array_partial_sort_inplace always walks the full candidate array (a std::partial_sort for npartial <= 128, otherwise a two-pass 128-bucket histogram over logits clamped to [-10,+10]), llama_sampler_temp_impl scans the whole array for the max even at temp = 0, and llama_sample_dist builds a std::discrete_distribution over an iterator spanning the array. Measured confirmation: top_k=1 changes throughput by nothing (711 vs 717 tok/s at 32 slots) while partial_sort is still 12.7% of in-gap CPU. So the cost model is O(n_vocab) per step, times batch, times fp32 width - with NO arithmetic-intensity saving anywhere, because the array is walked twice (once for the histogram/partition, once for the distribution) at 4 bytes per element on a single core.
scales_with: vocab_size n_vocab (the entire cost is O(n_vocab) per step per sequence; 152064 for Qwen2.5, 128256 for Llama-3-8B, 32000 for Llama-2 - a 4.75x spread between models that a batch-1 benchmark would otherwise look identical)

batch_size (the D2H payload and the host walk are both linear in live sequences: 608.3 KB at 1 slot, 16,157.4 KB at 32 slots - this class is the one piece of per-token work that gets WORSE with concurrency, unlike decode_gemm whose AI = B improves)
logits dtype (fp32 doubles both the transfer and the host walk versus bf16; vLLM's sampler does an unconditional logits.to(torch.float32) every step even when the model emitted bf16)
num_sampled_candidates / top_k (NOT a cost lever on the host path - llama.cpp's partition and temp scan are full-array; measured top_k=1 changes throughput by <1%)
host CPU single-core performance (this is a single-threaded host cost inside the step's critical path; the repro host was an Intel Xeon E5-2673 v4 @ 2.30 GHz)
whether sampling runs on device or on host (backend sampling removes the transfer entirely and drops the sampler's share of in-gap host time from 58.6% to 1.0%)
speculative draft_k (backend sampling must then run one graph row per OUTPUT rather than per sequence, and needs a temporary RNG so rejected tokens do not advance the rng)

flop_classes.name: Hybrid attention-SSM KV cache sizing: how many SSM layers vs attention layers and what the KV-per-token becomes
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: In a hybrid model with A attention layers and S SSM layers, the KV cache per token is A * num_kv_heads * head_dim * 2 * 2 bytes (only attention layers contribute). The SSM layers contribute a fixed per-sequence state of S * d_inner * N * 2 bytes, independent of context. The KV-per-token is therefore A/(A+S) of a pure-attention model's KV-per-token. For Nemotron-H-8B (4 attention, 48 Mamba): KV-per-token = 4 * 8 * 128 * 2 * 2 = 16,384 bytes = 16 KiB/token. A pure-attention model with the same 52 layers would have 52 * 8 * 128 * 2 * 2 = 212,992 bytes = 208 KiB/token. The reduction is 13x. But the SSM state is 48 * 8192 * 128 * 2 = 100,663,296 bytes = 96 MiB per sequence. At 8K context, the attention KV is 8K * 16 KiB = 128 MiB, already exceeding the SSM state. At 128K context, the attention KV is 128K * 16 KiB = 2 GiB, while the SSM state remains 96 MiB. The crossover point where SSM state exceeds attention KV is at context = S * d_inner * N * 2 / (A * num_kv_heads * head_dim * 2 * 2) = 48 * 8192 * 128 * 2 / (4 * 8 * 128 * 2 * 2) = 100,663,296 / 16,384 = 6,144 tokens. Below 6K context, the attention KV is smaller; above 6K, the SSM state is smaller.
scales_with: num_attention_layers / num_ssm_layers ratio (the primary design knob)
context_length (attention KV grows linearly, SSM state is constant)
batch_size (both grow linearly, but SSM state does not amortize)
ssm_state_size N and d_inner
num_kv_heads and head_dim for the attention layers

flop_classes.name: Image tiling and visual token KV cache cost
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Image tiling multiplies visual token count by the number of tiles. For a 4-tile image (2x2 grid), the LLM sees 4x the visual tokens. KV cache cost scales linearly with token count: KV_bytes = num_layers * num_kv_heads * head_dim * 2 * bytes_per_element. For a 7B model with 28 layers, 4 KV heads, 128 head_dim, bf16: 28*4*128*2*2 = 57,344 B/token. A 4-tile image at 448x448 (256 tokens per tile) = 1024 visual tokens = 57.3 MB of KV cache. A single 1024x1024 tile (Pixtral) = 4096 tokens = 229 MB of KV cache. The KV cache cost of visual tokens can exceed the model weights themselves.
scales_with: number of tiles (linear)
tokens per tile (linear)
num_layers (linear)
num_kv_heads (linear)
head_dim (linear)
bytes_per_element (linear - bf16=2, fp8=1)

flop_classes.name: KV-cache offload to a CPU/DRAM tier: bytes over PCIe, why it is bandwidth-bound, and when it beats recompute
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: AI = 0 in the strict sense - offload is a DMA copy with no arithmetic - so cost = KV bytes / PCIe bandwidth, and the useful question is never 'how fast is the copy' but 'is the copy cheaper than the recompute it replaces'. That comparison is a flop-versus-byte trade between two different roofs: recomputing a KV block costs ~2 x active_params x block_tokens FLOPs on the compute roof, while loading it costs C_block bytes over the PCIe roof. vLLM's docs make offload DMA-based and asynchronous ('Transfers between GPU and CPU use DMA (cudaMemcpyAsync) and run asynchronously alongside model computation, so offloading adds minimal CPU- and GPU-core overhead'), which is what makes the offload direction nearly free and the load direction the one that costs TTFT. The vendor's own measured claim is a ratio, not a bandwidth: loading from the CPU tier 'reduces TTFT by X2-X22' depending on prompt size (H100, 500GB DRAM, GPU prefix caching disabled so CPU hits are isolated).
scales_with: kv_bytes_resident (linear in context_length x live sequences - offload is a capacity mechanism, so the volume is whatever does not fit in HBM)
pcie_generation_and_width (Gen4 x16 vs Gen5 x16 is roughly a 2x difference and it is the dominant term in the load path)
block_size / blocks_per_chunk (larger chunks amortise per-transfer overhead into larger, more efficient host I/Os)
host_dram_capacity (how much can be kept resident rather than staged)
gpu_preemption_rate (the win case: preempted sequences would otherwise recompute)
tier_depth (anything below the CPU primary tier costs two hops, since only CPU has direct GPU access)

flop_classes.name: KV cache movement: block copy, prefix sharing, prefill-to-decode handoff, and offload
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Pure data movement, AI = 0 - no flops at all, so every definition of this class is a bandwidth or interconnect problem. Volume per token is 2 (K and V) x num_kv_heads x head_dim x layers x kv_dtype_bytes; for a 32-layer, hidden-4096, GQA-8-head, bf16 model that is on the order of hundreds of KB per token. At a 32k context that is several GB of KV per sequence, which is why PagedAttention's near-zero-waste block management was worth 2-4x end-to-end throughput at the same latency vs Orca and FasterTransformer, more so at longer sequences and larger models (arXiv 2309.06180). The copy that dominates is not the write of new KV but the movement implied by preemption, rescheduling, prefix sharing, and multi-node sharding - each of which is a full pass over the cache.
scales_with: context_length (cache bytes grow linearly; this is the whole story)
batch_size x live_sequences (total cache footprint)
num_kv_heads (GQA shrinks it directly)
kv_cache_dtype
tensor_parallel_degree (a KV block sharded across N devices must be gathered before attention, adding N-1 transfers per block read)
prefix sharing rate (how much can be deduplicated instead of copied)

flop_classes.name: llama.cpp MMQ: INT8 activation quantization with per-arch tile configs, no tensor cores
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: A different answer to the same problem, and the reason llama.cpp's quantized numbers are not comparable to Marlin's or Machete's. MMQ quantizes the ACTIVATIONS to q8_1 blocks of 32 elements and performs the dot product in INT8 accumulating to INT32, using DP4A where available. So the multiply-accumulates are integer SIMT instructions, not tensor-core MMAs - the FLOP:byte ratio the tensor cores exploit is not available at all. It buys portability: per-arch config headers exist for Ampere, Blackwell, CDNA, GCN, RDNA2/3/4/5 and Pascal (DP4A), the block size is a fixed 32 with three different scale/data layouts, MMQ_ITER_K is 256 (512 for FP4) and MMQ_NWARPS is 8. Notably, DP4A is used only while fp16 tensor cores are unavailable or the batch is small (MMQ_DP4A_MAX_BATCH_SIZE 64), which is itself a tensor-core-adjacent threshold.
scales_with: batch_size
weight quantization type (a dedicated block_fp4_mmq type exists)
num_SMs (MMQ_NWARPS 8 per block is a fixed occupancy choice)
arch (per-arch tile configs differ)

flop_classes.name: KV-cache tiering (LMCache): deciding, outside the kernel, how much KV the attention kernel must read from HBM
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Not an arithmetic mechanism at all, which is why it matters as a kernel-level decision input. A KV tier between the GPU and host/remote storage changes how many bytes the decode attention kernel pulls from HBM, but it does not change the attention FLOPs at all. The strongest version of the effect is prefix reuse: if a shared prefix KV is resident in GPU memory because a cache tier kept it there, every request reading that prefix does zero HBM traffic for it. So the practical AI of decode attention is set by cache hit rate, not only by the kernel's tiling.
scales_with: context_length
prefix sharing rate across requests
GPU HBM capacity (the tier only helps once the hot set fits)
batch_size

flop_classes.name: Logit processors in the decode loop: penalties, min_p, bias, min_tokens, and the host work they force
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Logit processors are not one cost, they are two, and conflating them is the whole reason this class has been invisible. (a) DEVICE half: each active processor is one or more full-width passes over the [B, V] logits tensor. vLLM's shipped MinPLogitsProcessor.apply does softmax over dim=-1, amax over dim=-1, mul_, a comparison, and masked_fill_ in place - four to five full V-wide passes at fp32, per step, whenever ANY request in the batch sets min_p. At V = 128256 that is 4-5 x 501.0 KiB = 2.0-2.5 MB read plus the same written per row, against a Llama-3-8B batch-1 step that streams 2*8.03e9 = 16.06 GB of weights: the processor is 0.012-0.016% of the step's bytes, so on the device it is again nearly free. LogitBias is a single scatter-add (V-independent work over |bias| ids). MinTokens mutates O(|min_tokens|) positions. So the arithmetic intensity is the same ~1 flop/byte as plain sampling and the DEVICE answer is the same: negligible. (b) HOST half, which is not negligible at all: vLLM's apply_all_penalties takes the per-request output_token_ids PYTHON lists every step, pads them into a CPU int64 tensor on PINNED memory with pad=vocab_size, and uploads it non-blocking - so the payload is max_output_len x batch x 8 B, rebuilt and re-uploaded every step, growing as sequences lengthen, and it also fills -1 placeholders (async-scheduling rows that will not be penalised) with vocab_size to keep the scatter valid. Add the batch bookkeeping: min_p state is a CPU-side mirror (min_p_cpu numpy view, an O(batch) min_p_count maintained from added/removed/moved batch events), and logit_bias state is a Python dict rebuilt into three device tensors via async_tensor_h2d whenever any request's bias changes. The published end-to-end measurement is unambiguous about which half binds: vLLM v0.6.2 through v0.7.2 on A100-SXM4-80GB with Llama-3-8B-Instruct, tp=1, penalty parameters set, 2000 prompt + 200 output tokens per request at 2000-4000 users' arrival scale - TPOT went 0.0356 s at 30 users to 0.24 s, 0.0659 -> 0.275 at 50, 0.115 -> 0.314 at 100, 0.208 -> 0.544 at 190, while generated TPM fell 33.3K -> 5.24K at 30 users and 53.1K -> 17.4K at 190, CPU core usage went 1.43 -> 3.7-4.0 cores (the pod cap) and GPU utilisation 81-100% -> 0-25%. v0.6.0 was fine, so the regression window is specific.
scales_with: batch_size (INVERSELY in the published failure - the regression appears only above batch ~20; below that the same penalty path is free. Device passes are linear in B, host bookkeeping linear in B)
output sequence length so far (the penalties upload payload is max_output_len x batch x 8 B, so it grows every step - the worst possible scaling for a per-step cost)
num_processors_enabled (each is a separate pass or a separate launch; the launch count is what the launch_overhead bound names)
num_stop_and_stateful_ids (min_tokens, stop-token ids, logit_bias entries drive a scatter whose width is set by request content, not by vocab)
vocab_size V (device passes only: 128256 for Llama-3-8B, 152064 for Qwen2.5, 32000 for Llama-2)

whether the processor is argmax-invariant (min_p returns True, logit_bias False - engines use this to skip the processor entirely for greedy requests, which is why enabling penalties can be free in a greedy-only deployment)
host CPU speed and pinned-memory availability (the upload and the Python list->tensor padding are host costs on the step's critical path)

flop_classes.name: Long-context RAG ingest: a 32k document prefilled into a KV cache (attention-dominated, plus the KV write)
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Long-context ingest is the most compute-dense step in the entire serving stack, and the arithmetic says so unambiguously. Take Llama-3-8B from its own config.json (d=4096, 14336 intermediate, 32 layers, 32 query / 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, vocab 128256): P_layer = d*n_q*dh + 2*d*n_kv*dh + n_q*dh*d + 3*d*dffn = 4096*4096 + 2*4096*1024 + 4096*4096 + 3*4096*14336 = 16.78M + 8.39M + 16.78M + 176.16M = 218.1M per layer; total non-embedding = 218,103,808 * 32 = 6.98B, plus untied embeddings 2*4096*128256 = 1.05B, giving 8.03B, which reproduces the released parameter count exactly. Ingesting L = 32768 tokens: GEMM flops = 2*P_total*L = 2*8.03e9*32768 = 526 TFLOP; causal attention flops = 2*n_q*dh*L^2 = 2*4096*32768^2 = 8.80 TFLOP, i.e. attention is only 8.80/(526+8.80) = 1.7% of prefill flops - the GEMMs dominate by ~60x, which is the opposite of the intuition that 'long context = attention-bound'. The attention share is set by L* = P_layer/(n_q*dh) = 218,103,808/4096 = 53,248 tokens: at 32k we are still BELOW the crossover. For the same L on a 70B-class model the share falls further (Llama-2-70B, GQA-8, d=8192, 28672 intermediate, 80 layers: P_layer = 855.6M, L* = 855,638,016/8192 = 104,448 tokens, attention = 17.6 TFLOP against 4,486 TFLOP of GEMM = 0.4%). So a 32k RAG ingest is a prefill_GEMM problem wearing an attention hat. The KV WRITE is a separate, pure-store term with AI = 0: bytes = 2 (K and V) * 32 layers * 8 KV heads * 128 head_dim * 2 bytes * 32768 tokens = 4.29 GB = 4.00 GiB. Whole-step AI including that write = (534.6 TFLOP)/(4.29 GB) = 124,600 flop/byte, 422x above H100's 295.4 ridge. The write itself costs 4.29 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 1.28 ms on H100, 5.24 ms on TPU v5e (819 GB/s) and 4.26 ms on RTX 4090 (1008 GB/s) - against 1061 ms for the GEMM+attention flops at 50% of H100's 989.5 TFLOPS. So the store is 0.1-0.5% of the step on every part and is never the bottleneck; it only becomes one when the ingest is SHARDED across devices or offloaded, which converts it into kv_transfer.
scales_with: context_length (quadratic in attention flops, linear in GEMM flops; the share only becomes large past L* = P_layer/(n_q*dh), which is 53k tokens for an 8B-class model and 104k for a 70B-class one)

model_width_per_layer (through L*: a wider MLP per layer pushes the attention crossover further out, so a 70B model at 32k is LESS attention-bound than a 7B model at 32k - counterintuitive but it follows from the parameter ratio)
gqa_group_ratio g (multiplies prefill attention AI by g, cutting KV bytes by g; does not change attention flops)
num_retrieved_documents (total ingest length is the sum of chunk lengths; flops are additive so ingest scales linearly in corpus size)

tensor_parallel_degree / sequence_parallelism (once one device cannot hold the cache, a ring all-gather over the sequence makes the interconnect part of this class - see tensor-parallel-allreduce and the Ring Attention record)
kv_cache_dtype (halving KV bytes halves the store term and halves resident capacity, but is irrelevant to the compute-bound part)

flop_classes.name: Low-entropy / near-greedy decode: when the distribution collapses, which flops can be skipped
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Sampling's cost is fixed by vocabulary size, not by how peaked the distribution is - and that is the central fact about low-entropy decode. Per token the sampler must read the logits out of HBM (2*V bytes at bf16, 4*V at fp32) before it can discover that the answer was obvious the whole time. For Llama-3-8B with V = 128,256 and d = 4096: logits = 2*128256 = 256.5 KiB/token in bf16, against a step that reads 2*P = 2*8.03e9 = 16.06 GB of weights, so the logits are 0.0016% of the step's HBM traffic. The arithmetic is blunt: the expensive part (reading the weights to produce the logits) is 100% of the work, and the part that collapses (choosing among the logits) is 0.0016%. This means the obvious optimization - detect a peaked distribution and skip sampling - cannot buy more than about one part in 60,000, because the expensive work has already happened by the time you know the distribution is peaked. The one exception worth naming is the LM HEAD itself, which is a real weight matrix of 2*d*V = 2*4096*128256 = 1.051 GB, i.e. 6.54% of a Llama-3-8B decode step's bytes and 6.54% of its flops (2*d*V = 1.051 GFLOP against 2*P = 16.1 GFLOP). For a large-vocab model the LM head is the one place where a peaked distribution could enable real work reduction, and even there the reduction requires skipping the projection, not skipping the softmax.
scales_with: vocab_size V (logit bytes scale linearly: 2*V at bf16, 4*V at fp32 - 250.5 KiB and 501.0 KiB per token for V=128256)
entropy_of_the_distribution (NOT a cost driver: bytes must be read before the entropy is known, so a greedy token costs the same as a uniform one)
candidate_set_size after top-k/top-p (the one knob that reduces actual work: a top-256 candidate set reads 2*d*256 = 2.10 MB instead of 1.051 GB of head, a 500x reduction of that term)
whether_the_model_uses_a_large_vocab (Llama-3-8B's 128256 vocab makes the LM head 6.54% of the step; Llama-2's 32000 vocab with d=4096 makes it 2*4096*32000 = 262 MB against 13.48 GB = 1.94%)
logits_dtype (fp32 logits double the read for no benefit in a greedy path)
batch_size (each sequence pays its own 2*V bytes even though the sampler is one kernel, so sampling is as batch-invariant as decode_attention)

flop_classes.name: Machete weight-only 4-bit GEMM: CUTLASS 3.x tiles plus an offline prepacked int4 B operand, Hopper only
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Same class of claim as Marlin - no FLOP change, dequant removed from the runtime path - but achieved differently: Machete keeps CUTLASS's Hopper WGMMA tensor-core mainloop and changes the B OPERAND LAYOUT instead. The kernel source is explicit that LayoutB is ColumnMajor only 'not actually used since B has the prepacked layout', and the tile K extent is computed as 128*8/sizeof_bits<MmaType> so the same integer-tile arithmetic is expressed in the quantized bit width. Weights, group scales and group zeros are prepacked offline into the exact fragment organization WGMMA consumes, so the inner loop issues MMA on already-correctly-laid-out data. Alignments are all 128-bit. The arithmetic consequence: this is a tensor-core bf16/fp16 GEMM over int4 weights dequantized into the MMA fragments on the fly, NOT a hardware int4 tensor-core path - there is no int4 MMA instruction being used.
scales_with: batch_size (M dimension; the kernel is a GEMM so small M is inefficient)
group size (gated by query_machete_supported_group_sizes)
hidden_width

flop_classes.name: Marlin weight-only INT4 GEMM: repacking so dequant is free and tensor cores stay saturated
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Marlin does not change the FLOPs; it removes the dequantization tax by moving it offline and restructuring the kernel so dequant and MMA are ordered so neither pipeline stalls. The author's framing is a ratio: 'as long as we perform less than 25-50 (tensor core) multiply-accumulates per 4-bit quantized weight' - i.e. per 4-bit weight element, not per block - the FLOP:byte ratio of the GPU permits near-ideal 4x speedup, and the theoretical benefit of weight-only quantization should extend to batch sizes 4-8x larger than prior kernels achieved. The mechanism is fourfold: (1) asynchronous global weight loads issued ahead of all compute, including activation loads, with an eviction-immediate cache policy so one-shot weights do not pollute L2; (2) quantized weights AND group scales reshuffled offline into a layout that dequantizes directly into tensor-core organization, so no separate dequant pass exists; (3) careful interleaving of dequant and tensor-core instructions so both pipelines stay saturated; (4) striped partitioning of the output so real (smaller) matrices and varied GPUs still perform well. The payoff is stated as essentially ideal speedup up to the maximum possible 3.87x at all batch sizes, versus prior kernels hitting ~3.87x at batch 1 and degrading quickly as batch grows.
scales_with: batch_size (the whole design target - hold the 4x speedup as batch grows)
group size (128 in the author's benchmarks; scales add 0.125 bits of storage overhead at g128)
weight shape (striped partitioning is what makes small matrices work)
GPU clock (the author finds reduced clocks hurt prior kernels' relative speedup but not Marlin's)

flop_classes.name: The MLA up-projection that absorption removes: recomputing K and V from the cached latent
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: This is the cost MLA hides, and it only appears if you decline the absorption trick. DeepSeek-V2 states that during inference 'since W_UK can be absorbed into W_Q, and W_UV can be absorbed into W_O, we even do not need to compute keys and values out for attention'. Do the naive thing instead and up-project the cached latent every decode step: for DeepSeek-V3's shape (n_h=128, d_nope=128, d_rh=64, d_h(v)=128, d_c=512) that is W_UK = 128*192*512 = 12,582,912 elements and W_UV = 128*128*512 = 8,388,608 elements, 20,971,520 elements = 41.9 MB of bf16 weights read per layer per step. The flops are 2*20,971,520 = 41.9 MFLOP against 41.9 MB, so AI = 1 flop/byte - exactly the bandwidth-bound weight-GEMM regime, and this repeats for all 61 layers: ~2.56 GB of weight traffic per decode step that the absorbed form does not pay. The break-even context length is where the recompute cost exceeds the cache it saves: 41.9 MB of weights amortises over (d_c+d_rh)*2 = 1,152 bytes/token of cache saved, so ~36,400 cached tokens. Below that, recomputing is pure loss; above it, if you are memory- rather than bandwidth-constrained, a non-absorbed MLA kernel can be a reasonable trade. RoPE is what forces the issue: DeepSeek-V2 Sec 2.1.3 shows that with position-sensitive RoPE on the keys, W_UK cannot be absorbed into W_Q because 'a RoPE matrix related to the currently generating token will lie between W_Q and W_UK and matrix multiplication does not obey a commutative law' - and without absorption you 'must recompute the keys for all the prefix tokens during inference, which will significantly hinder the inference efficiency'.
scales_with: context_length (the up-projection win grows with prefix length, the absorbed form is flat)
num_layers (the weight traffic multiplies by layer count: 61x for DeepSeek-V3)
kv_lora_rank d_c (both the weight size and the cache saved scale with it)
num_attention_heads
batch_size (absorbed: AI flat in batch; unabsorbed: AI = 1 at any batch, so it is the same bandwidth trap at every scale)
